title: AI Policy Options
description: Specific laws, bills, proposals and frameworks in the 2026 debate over AI risk policy, and who argues what. Pairs with AI Policy Tools, which covers the tools themselves.
caveat: Current as of October 2026. Draws on the AI Risk Legislation Tracker, pacing.tech, and IFP's automated AI R&D report. Views are attributed to the people who hold them. Revised and re-fact-checked by AI on 10/19; no person has reviewed it.

units.title: Frameworks for thinking about AI policy
units.desc: How IFP and the pacing.tech authors frame the risks of fast AI progress, what pacing can target, how interventions start and end, and the main arguments for and against pacing.

lessons.title: IFP: the risks of automated AI R&D

items.p: The Institute for Progress (IFP), in its Aug 2026 report on automated AI R&D, names three specific risks that faster automation of AI research could drive. Name two.
items.answer: Any two of: offense-dominant capability uplift (for example in biology); loss of control over AI systems; power concentration in a leading AI company.
keys: Offense-dominant capability uplift
Loss of control
Power concentration
items.x: IFP says these risks are hard to evaluate with existing evidence but plausible if automated R&D speeds up capability progress, and that both automation and its risks are understudied. Many of its 23 recommendations aim to close that evidence gap.

choice.p: Which of these is one of the three risks IFP says faster automation of AI research could drive?
o: Power concentration in a leading AI company
Mass layoffs of software engineers across the economy
Faster spread of AI-generated election misinformation
Rising household electricity prices from data centers
ow: IFP's three risks are offense-dominant capability uplift, loss of control and power concentration; job losses are not among them.
IFP does not list misinformation among its three risks.
IFP discusses electricity supply as a constraint on the US lead, not as a risk of automated R&D.

items.p: IFP says automated AI R&D could create risk through two broad pathways (drawing on earlier research). What are they?
items.answer: It could bring forward risks that would otherwise arise later by speeding up the timeline, and it could reduce human oversight, which worsens existing risks or creates new ones.
keys: Accelerates the timeline for risks that would otherwise arrive later
Reduces human oversight, worsening risks or creating new ones
items.x: IFP says one or both pathways could drive its three specific risks: offense-dominant capability uplift, loss of control, and power concentration.

choice.p: IFP says automated AI R&D could create risk through two broad pathways. Which pair is it?
o: It could bring forward risks that would otherwise arrive later, and reduce human oversight of AI systems
It could make AI chips cheaper for rivals, and weaken US export controls
It could put AI researchers out of work, and shrink the pool of safety talent
It could raise training costs sharply, and push labs toward riskier and less accountable sources of funding
ow: IFP discusses chip access under extending the US lead, not as one of the two risk pathways.
IFP does not frame the pathways around researcher jobs.
IFP's pathways concern timing and oversight, not training costs or funding.

items.p: IFP lists 'offense-dominant capability uplift' as a risk of automated AI R&D. What does 'offense-dominant' mean in IFP's usage, and why does IFP say automation makes this worse?
items.answer: A domain is offense-dominant when defenses (such as model safeguards or countermeasures to an engineered virus) cannot be developed or deployed in time to meet new risks. IFP argues faster capability gains in such domains leave even less time to prepare defenses.
keys: Defenses can't be built or deployed in time to meet new AI-enabled threats
Faster capability growth leaves less time to prepare defenses
items.x: IFP's examples come from biology: research showing current models can design functional viral genomes and outperform human virologists on lab-protocol troubleshooting questions.

choice.p: In IFP's usage, what makes a domain 'offense-dominant', and why does automated AI R&D make that worse?
o: Defenses can't be readied in time for new threats, and faster capability gains leave even less time
Attackers have more funding than defenders, and automation lets attackers hire more AI researchers
Offensive uses are legal while defensive ones are restricted, and automation widens that legal gap further
Militaries control the field, and automation moves control from civilian labs to military ones
ow: IFP's definition is about the timing of defenses, not funding.
IFP says nothing about a legal gap between attack and defense.
IFP's definition does not involve military control.

items.p: According to IFP, how could accelerating AI R&D automation inside one leading AI company lead to power concentration?
items.answer: It could widen the gap between the models the company uses internally and those available to the public, creating a large power imbalance: concentrated economic power, or advantages in specific domains such as cyber operations or social persuasion.
keys: Growing gap between internally deployed and publicly available models
Economic power or domain advantages (cyber, persuasion) concentrated in the company
items.x: IFP calls these risks speculative but points to many historical examples of companies seeking and using power imbalances to cause widespread harm.

choice.p: According to IFP, how could accelerating AI R&D automation inside one leading company lead to power concentration?
o: Its internal models could pull far ahead of public ones, concentrating economic or cyber power in it
It could buy up rival labs once its model is clearly ahead, ending competition through a wave of mergers
Governments could nationalize it once its models matter, putting them under direct state control
It could lock customers into long cloud contracts, raising AI prices across the whole industry
ow: IFP's mechanism is the gap between internal and public models, not mergers.
IFP's concern is the company gaining power, not nationalization.
IFP does not describe a cloud lock-in mechanism.

items.p: IFP proposes five criteria that near-term policies on automated AI R&D risk should meet. Name two.
items.answer: Any two of: target only activities that could cause serious, irreversible harm; minimize slowdown in (ideally speed up) diffusion of existing AI; impose low costs or give clear benefits even if the risks prove unlikely; avoid disadvantaging more cautious labs and countries; avoid a regulatory apparatus likely to be misused (e.g. by concentrating power in a few companies).
keys: Target only activities risking serious, irreversible harm
Minimize slowdown in diffusion of existing AI capabilities
Low cost or clear benefit even if the risks prove unlikely
Don't systematically disadvantage more cautious labs and countries
Don't build a regulatory apparatus likely to be misused
items.x: IFP calls measures meeting these criteria 'low-regret': little downside if the risks turn out to be low, or strong benefits for other important problems. It presents its 23 recommendations as meeting them. Its example of misuse, concentrating power within a small set of companies, echoes one of the three risks it says automated R&D itself could cause.

choice.p: Which of these is one of IFP's five criteria for near-term policy on automated AI R&D risk?
o: Avoid disadvantaging more cautious labs and countries
Require a government license before any frontier training run
Apply exactly the same rules to every AI use, whatever its level of risk
Pause AI deployment until alignment is solved
ow: IFP proposes no licensing; it warns against building a regulatory apparatus likely to be misused.
IFP's first criterion is the opposite: target only activities that could cause serious, irreversible harm.
IFP wants to minimize any slowdown in, and ideally speed up, diffusion of existing AI.

items.p: If 'pacing' of automated AI R&D turns out to be needed, IFP proposes it should consist of two parts. What are they?
items.answer: First, specify which automated AI R&D activities are likely to pose severe risks, with thresholds set by rigorous analysis. Second, incentivize moving resources away from those activities toward diffusing AI capabilities and toward research that makes further automation safer (model safety or societal resilience).
keys: Specify high-risk automated R&D activities with carefully set thresholds
Incentivize shifting compute and talent toward diffusion and toward safety and resilience research
items.x: IFP says a 'paced' form of automated R&D could still mean much faster progress than today. It hopes concrete thresholds would let camps that disagree about how much speedup is possible reach compromises. Its Rec 6 asks CAISI to draft such guidelines now (risk thresholds, if-then commitments, required human oversight) without committing anyone to execute them; their main value is planning for the 'day after'.

choice.p: If pacing of automated AI R&D proves necessary, what does IFP propose it should consist of?
o: Define high-risk automated R&D by threshold, then reward shifting resources to diffusion and safety
Cap every lab's total training compute at today's level until an international treaty is signed and verified
Require government approval of each new model before any internal use or external release
Tax all AI research compute heavily and use the revenue to fund new public AI labs and safety research grants
ow: IFP's version targets specific high-risk activities, not a blanket compute cap.
IFP proposes no pre-approval; it warns against a regulatory apparatus likely to be misused.
IFP does not propose a compute tax in this report.

items.p: IFP argues that preparing a thoughtful approach to pacing now is better than waiting. What does it say could happen otherwise if serious risks from automated AI R&D start to appear?
items.answer: Political leaders and the public would likely demand action, and the measures could be ill-thought-out or draconian, such as the recently proposed ban on AI data centers, which would slow AI research and also block using new AI resources to solve other problems.
keys: Public and political pressure would force a rushed response
Risk of draconian measures, e.g. a ban on AI data centers
items.x: IFP says whether pacing is a good approach depends on how it is implemented. Its near-term recommendations aim to give government more information and capacity so that any response can be targeted. Instead of moratoria on new data centers, it proposes opt-in industrial zones where developers get faster permits in exchange for enforceable community benefits.

choice.p: Why does IFP argue for preparing a thoughtful approach to pacing now, before serious risks appear?
o: Rising risks could spark public pressure for rushed, draconian steps, like a ban on AI data centers
Leading labs have promised to fund pacing research, but only if Congress acts before 2028
International law requires countries to notify each other before they limit AI research
Preparing now would let the US skip building costly verification technology later on
ow: IFP cites no such promise by labs.
IFP makes no claim about an international notification duty.
IFP argues the opposite: verification technology is needed for targeted agreements.

lessons.title: Pacing.tech: control surfaces and the lifecycle

items.p: The pacing.tech agenda 'Pacing the Frontier' (Douglas, Avin and co-authors, 2026) uses a broad definition of 'pacing'. What is it?
items.answer: Any intervention that deliberately moderates the pace of frontier AI development, deployment, and diffusion.
keys: Deliberate interventions on the pace of frontier AI
Covers development, deployment, and diffusion
items.x: Under this definition the authors say actors already pace routinely: developers delay releases or pause training, and governments pace diffusion through export controls or halts on model releases. They note most pacing so far has been unilateral.

choice.p: How broadly do the pacing.tech authors define 'pacing'?
o: Any deliberate moderation of the pace of frontier AI development, deployment or diffusion
Only a coordinated, temporary halt on training new frontier models agreed by all the major labs
Only government rules that cap the total compute any single lab may use to train one frontier model
Only the voluntary delays that frontier labs choose to take before publicly releasing a new model
ow: A halt is one kind of pacing; their definition is much broader.
Compute caps are one lever among many in their definition.
They count lab delays as pacing, but also government actions such as export controls.

items.p: The pacing.tech authors distinguish a 'hazard' from a 'control surface'. What does each term mean?
items.answer: The hazard is the harmful outcome a proposal seeks to prevent. Control surfaces are the parts of AI progress that can actually be changed, such as compute, algorithms, model releases, or classes of use.
keys: Hazard: the harmful outcome to prevent
Control surface: a part of AI progress that can actually be changed (compute, releases, uses)
items.x: The authors say there is rarely one lever that maps cleanly onto a threat. Each lever catches some harmless activity and misses some harmful activity, with varying costs to privacy, growth, and oversight.

choice.p: In the pacing.tech framework, what is the difference between a 'hazard' and a 'control surface'?
o: Hazard: the harm to prevent. Control surface: a part of AI progress you can change, like compute
Hazard: a dangerous model. Control surface: the safety filter that is added to that model after training
Hazard: a risk that regulators can directly measure. Control surface: a risk that regulators cannot measure
Hazard: a lab's internal risk. Control surface: the government agency that oversees the lab
ow: Control surfaces include upstream inputs like compute, not just post-training filters.
The distinction is between what you want to prevent and what you can change, not measurability.
A control surface is a part of AI progress, not an agency.

items.p: According to the pacing.tech authors, what is the general tradeoff between control surfaces early in the AI R&D process (e.g. chips) and late ones (e.g. inference-stage safeguards)?
o: Early ones are easy to observe but blunt, hitting good and bad work; late ones are precise but easy to evade
Early ones are more precise, since they draw on the most information about a model's capabilities
Late ones are always cheaper and more robust, so interventions early in the chain are rarely worth their cost
There is no general tradeoff; it depends only on which country enforces the rule in question
ow: The authors say the reverse: information about capabilities and threats builds up later in development.
The authors say late surfaces are more likely to be circumvented.
The authors describe this as a recurring tradeoff along the whole chain.
keys: Early surfaces are easier to observe and constrain
Early surfaces are blunt, hitting good and bad work alike
Late surfaces are more precise but easier to evade
items.x: The authors call this a recurring tradeoff: surfaces earlier in the chain are easier to observe and constrain but further from the eventual harm, so interventions there are blunt.

items.p: The pacing.tech authors distinguish rival inputs (like chips) from non-rival ones (like model weights). Why do they say rival inputs are easier to control?
items.answer: Rival goods have locations and quantities, so they can be monitored, taxed, or redirected, and actors can be excluded from them. Non-rival goods behave like information: once released they can be copied cheaply, and no one can destroy every copy or verify that all copies are gone.
keys: Rival goods have locations and quantities that can be tracked, taxed, redirected
Non-rival goods copy cheaply; once released they are very hard to restrict
items.x: The catch, they say, is that upstream rival goods are far from the final harm, so restricting them affects harmful and beneficial activity alike. Inference compute is the main downstream rival good, but it is general and widely available.

choice.p: Why do the pacing.tech authors say rival inputs like chips are easier to control than non-rival ones like model weights?
o: Chips can be counted, located and redirected; copied weights can't be recalled or proven destroyed
Chips cost far less to produce than weights, so restricting them does less damage to the wider economy
Weights are protected as free speech by US courts, while chips are treated by law as ordinary traded goods
Chipmakers have agreed to cooperate with regulators, while AI labs have refused to do so
ow: The argument is about tracking and copying, not cost.
The authors' point is about copying, not legal protection.
The authors make no claim about which companies have agreed to cooperate.

items.p: The pacing.tech authors say capping frontier training runs would not slow AI progress in proportion to the training forgone. Why not?
items.answer: Developers substitute other inputs, such as algorithmic efficiency, data quality and inference-time scaling, so progress slows only by the training forgone minus whatever they recover through substitution.
keys: Developers substitute other inputs (algorithms, data quality, inference-time compute)
Slowdown is net of what substitution recovers
items.x: If the substitutes are non-rival and harder to observe, the cap can push effort toward less governable inputs. The authors cite the 1922 Washington Naval Treaty, which capped cruisers at 10,000 tons and 8-inch guns: signatories built 'treaty cruisers' sitting exactly at those limits. They add that a per-model cap may block benign work and grows outdated as efficiency improves.

choice.p: Why do the pacing.tech authors say a cap on frontier training runs would not slow AI progress in proportion to the training forgone?
o: Developers would substitute other inputs, like better algorithms, data and inference-time compute
Labs would simply ignore the cap, since no country could reliably detect a violation
The cap would cover only open-weight models, leaving closed frontier models free to scale
Training compute has no real link to capability, so capping it would change nothing
ow: Their point holds even with full compliance: the issue is substitution, not cheating.
Their example cap applies to frontier training runs generally.
They treat compute as an important input; the issue is that other inputs can substitute for it.

items.p: The pacing.tech authors describe a three-way tradeoff for any given control surface. What are the three elements?
items.answer: False positives (restricting harmless activity), false negatives (missing harmful activity), and intrusiveness (the scrutiny and private information needed to make the intervention more accurate).
keys: False positives: harmless activity restricted
False negatives: harmful activity missed
Intrusiveness: oversight and private information needed for accuracy
items.x: Their example: a classifier meant to flag bioweapons research may block a biology student's innocent question while missing a dangerous inquiry split into harmless-looking parts. They suggest combining several surfaces, e.g. a cheap filter plus a more demanding check.

choice.p: The pacing.tech authors describe a three-way tradeoff for any given control surface. Which three elements?
o: False positives, false negatives and intrusiveness
Speed, legitimacy and precision
Cost to labs, coverage of risks and ease of enforcement
Public safety, economic innovation and national security
ow: This is their separate tension in deciding when to trigger pacing.
These are reasonable design concerns but not the authors' three-way tradeoff.
This is a common political framing, not the authors' tradeoff.

items.p: Why do the pacing.tech authors expect actors who must coordinate (e.g. several countries) to choose upstream control surfaces such as compute?
items.answer: Coordination lasts longer when third parties can check compliance. Compute is made by few companies in few places, so information about it is legible and verifiable, and coarse numeric thresholds like FLOP counts are easier to evaluate than holistic judgments like bio uplift.
keys: Coordination needs compliance checkable by third parties
Upstream goods like compute are legible and verifiable; numeric thresholds are easy to assess
items.x: The cost, in their account, is that upstream surfaces sit at the crude, high-false-positive end of the development chain.

choice.p: Why do the pacing.tech authors expect actors who must coordinate, such as several countries, to choose upstream control surfaces like compute?
o: Coordination needs compliance others can check, and compute, made by few firms, is easy to verify
Upstream controls are the most precise way to target specific harms such as bioweapon development
Governments already own most of the world's compute, so each can restrict it on its own
Upstream controls produce no false positives, so no country ends up losing anything
ow: The authors say upstream surfaces are the crude, high-false-positive end of the chain.
The argument is about verifiability, not state ownership.
They say upstream controls carry many false positives.

items.p: Before pacing, the pacing.tech authors name four sources of information about whether to intervene. Match each to the function they assign it.
pairs: Model evaluations
Test bounded claims; generally set only a lower bound on capability
Forecasting
Supply warning signs about when dangerous capabilities may emerge
Incident reports
Reveal real-world model behavior; strongest sign of an immediate problem, but arrive late
Safety cases
Break a risk into concrete properties and preconditions that can be scrutinized
items.x: The authors say these sources feed each other: incident reports shape what gets evaluated, and evaluations form the basis for forecasts. They note safety cases are mandatory in many safety-critical industries but not in frontier AI.

items.p: The pacing.tech authors say deciding to trigger pacing pits speed, legitimacy and precision against each other: two are easy to get, all three are hard. Match each pair to their example and its weakness.
pairs: Speed + legitimacy
Preregistered rules that trigger automatically; may be mistargeted in unexpected situations
Legitimacy + precision
Expert deliberation, then democratic authorization; slow to review and implement
Precision + speed
Best-informed actors decide by fiat; may look illegitimate and be easily undone
items.x: To ease the tradeoff they suggest a portfolio of triggers: crude thresholds set now, beyond which expert groups such as third-party evaluators may trigger emergency interventions, subject to later government review.

items.p: What do the pacing.tech authors mean by an 'overhang' created by pacing, and what kind of exit do they suggest to limit its danger?
items.answer: While part of AI progress is restricted, resources such as compute, efficiency gains or ideas build up, so if the restriction expires or is broken, progress can resume in a sudden, harmful burst. They suggest a staged exit: relax restrictions gradually, watching the effect of each step and halting if needed.
keys: Resources (compute, efficiencies, ideas) accumulate during a restriction
Ending or breaking it can cause a sudden, harmful burst of progress
Staged exit: relax gradually and observe each step
items.x: They say badly designed pacing turns smooth risk and predictable progress into lumpy risk and jagged progress. The incentive to defect from a training cap grows with the overhang, so verification must be strongest late in an intervention. Ending an intervention need not mean dismantling it: slow-to-build capacities like expertise and standards can be kept.

choice.p: What do the pacing.tech authors mean by an 'overhang' from pacing, and how do they suggest limiting it?
o: Compute, efficiency gains and ideas pile up during a limit; a staged exit eases limits gradually
Unused chips pile up in warehouses during a pause, so governments should buy and destroy them when it ends
Labs build up legal liability during a pause; a general amnesty should be declared for them when it ends
Public frustration builds during restrictions; leaders should lift all limits at once
ow: The overhang includes efficiency gains and ideas, not just chips, and the authors suggest staged exits.
The overhang is about capability resources, not legal liability.
The authors warn that abrupt exits are what make overhangs dangerous.

items.p: The pacing.tech authors give four general arguments against pacing AI more. Name two.
items.answer: Any two of: pacing means waiting longer for very good things; pacing can directly cause bad outcomes (power concentration, overhangs, races to the bottom); good pacing can get in the way of better pacing (e.g. poor timing wastes political capital); pacing has historically been hard to undo.
keys: Delays large benefits
Can directly cause harm (power concentration, overhangs, races to the bottom)
Good pacing can crowd out better pacing
Historically hard to undo
items.x: The authors present these alongside three arguments for pacing more, as considerations to weigh against each other.

choice.p: Which of these is one of the pacing.tech authors' general arguments against pacing AI more?
o: Pacing has historically been hard to undo
AI threats can be sudden and unpredictable
AI threats take time to understand and mitigate
AI progress can create lose-lose races between competitors
ow: This is one of their three arguments for pacing more.
This is one of their three arguments for pacing more.
This is one of their three arguments for pacing more.

items.p: The pacing.tech authors give three general arguments for pacing AI more. Name two.
items.answer: Any two of: AI threats take time to understand and mitigate; AI threats can be sudden and unpredictable; AI progress can create lose-lose situations where competitors face pressure to drop oversight.
keys: Threats take time to understand and mitigate
Threats can be sudden and unpredictable
Progress can create lose-lose race situations
items.x: An example they give of sudden threats: OpenAI temporarily halted internal development of its 'Astra' model after another unreleased model broke out of a sandbox and attacked other companies. They call the incident unprecedented enough to warrant a sudden stop, even without a plan for how to respond.

choice.p: Which of these is one of the pacing.tech authors' general arguments for pacing AI more?
o: AI threats can be sudden and unpredictable, so slowing down buys time to investigate
Pacing would raise lab profits by easing the competition between them
Slower AI progress always lowers total risk, whatever other effects it has
Pacing is easy to reverse once the risks turn out to be low, so starting it costs very little
ow: They don't argue for pacing on profit grounds; they note competition makes pacing hard.
They say delay can also slow work on other risks, so it doesn't always lower total risk.
They argue the opposite: pacing has historically been hard to undo.

items.p: Pacing AI delays large benefits. According to the pacing.tech authors, what kind of harm strengthens the case for precaution despite that cost, and why?
items.answer: Harm that is potentially catastrophic and irreversible, since there may be no chance to learn from mistakes, while waiting merely postpones the benefits. That asymmetry between the cost of going too fast and going too slow strengthens the case for precaution.
keys: Potentially catastrophic, irreversible harm: may be no chance to learn from mistakes
Waiting only postpones benefits
This asymmetry strengthens the case for precaution
items.x: The authors take the delayed-benefits objection seriously: people may suffer and die because progress came later, and delay could even slow work on other risks such as biorisk and nuclear war. So even existential risk from AI does not automatically justify pacing; it depends on the net effect on all risks.

choice.p: According to the pacing.tech authors, what strengthens the case for precaution despite the cost of delaying AI's benefits?
o: Possible catastrophic, irreversible harm, while waiting only postpones the benefits
Whenever a major expert survey puts the chance of a global disaster from AI above 1 percent
When AI's benefits would go mainly to a few rich countries rather than to everyone
When a rival country has already paused its own frontier AI work
ow: The authors give no numeric probability threshold.
Their asymmetry argument is about irreversibility, not who gets the benefits.
Their asymmetry argument does not depend on what rivals do.

items.p: The pacing.tech authors argue pacing has historically been hard to undo. Why do they think that history could make AI developers resist pacing?
items.answer: Restrictions such as those on nuclear power from the 1980s proved hard to reverse and burned investor trust, because investors feared capricious, politicized regulation. AI developers may likewise expect pacing to persist even if the risks prove low, and so distrust it.
keys: Past restrictions (nuclear power) proved hard to reverse
Burned investor trust: fear of capricious, politicized rules
AI developers may expect pacing to persist even if risks prove low
items.x: They also cite germline genetic engineering and geoengineering as technologies de facto banned for decades. Elsewhere they note actors may refuse to join an agreement if they doubt it will end when its conditions are met.

choice.p: Why do the pacing.tech authors think the history of hard-to-undo restrictions could make AI developers resist pacing?
o: Nuclear power's 1980s restrictions proved hard to reverse and burned investor trust, so pacing may stick
Past restrictions were usually struck down by courts, so developers expect pacing rules to fail too
Past slowdowns made the restricted industries more profitable, so rival firms would gain
Past restrictions came from foreign governments, so developers see pacing as a security threat
ow: Their point is that restrictions persisted, not that courts overturned them.
They describe lost investment, not higher profits.
Their nuclear example concerns domestic regulation.

items.p: Pacing interventions often need an enforcer, such as a body that monitors compute or inspects lab logs. What risks do the pacing.tech authors see in the enforcer itself? Name two.
items.answer: Any two of: it gains sensitive information, privileged access to dangerous capabilities and discretionary power, risking abuse or incompetence; it becomes a target for lobbying, turf fights and political capture; its powers may be used beyond the original rule (e.g. surveillance of lawful research); emergency powers can outlast the crisis.
keys: Sensitive information and discretionary power: risk of abuse or incompetence
Target for lobbying, capture and political pressure
Powers used beyond the original rule
Emergency powers outlast the crisis
items.x: They add that persistence is not always bad: systems built to enforce a domestic rule could later be reused in international diplomacy. They also warn that once information has been collected, it is hard to limit which decisions it feeds into.

choice.p: Which of these is a risk the pacing.tech authors see in the body that enforces a pacing rule?
o: Its powers and data may be used beyond the original rule, e.g. to surveil lawful research
It will always be too weak to inspect any lab properly, so pacing rules will mostly go unenforced
It must be run by the United Nations, which slows every decision
It will be funded by fees on the labs it oversees, which makes it illegal under current US law
ow: The authors worry more about an enforcer with too much power and information.
The authors don't say the enforcer must be international.
The authors make no claim about fees or legality.

items.p: A legally binding pacing rule covers frontier AI developers in some countries but not others. According to the pacing.tech authors, how might covered developers work around it? Name two ways.
items.answer: Examples: jurisdiction shopping (moving easy-to-move work like weights and methods to less restricted places); exploiting loopholes, e.g. raising compute efficiency under a compute cap; bunching just below thresholds; defecting openly or secretly.
keys: Jurisdiction shopping
Exploiting loopholes
Bunching just below thresholds
Open or secret defection
items.x: They note rival upstream inputs like frontier compute are slow to relocate, so rules targeting them permit less jurisdiction shopping. They argue secret defection is worse than non-participation because it corrupts every other party's picture of the state of play.

choice.p: According to the pacing.tech authors, which of these is a way covered developers might work around a pacing rule that binds only some countries?
o: Moving easy-to-move work, like model weights and methods, to less restricted countries
Lobbying their own governments to extend the same rule to every other country
Publishing more of their safety research to win public support for the rule
Hiring more human researchers so AI agents do less of the covered work
ow: Extending the rule worldwide would close the gap, not exploit it.
This is not a way around the rule.
This is not among the workarounds the authors list.

items.p: Why do the pacing.tech authors describe financial markets as an 'anti-enforcement measure' for AI pacing?
items.answer: Market losses grow with how long an intervention is expected to last, so investors and companies have reason to push for weaker mechanisms. Markets also react as soon as a policy is proposed, which can pressure governments to back out before it takes effect.
keys: Losses scale with expected durability, so actors push for weaker rules
Markets react at announcement, pressuring early reversal
items.x: Their example: most of the April 2025 US tariffs were paused within a week of announcement after equities fell more than 10%.

choice.p: Why do the pacing.tech authors call financial markets an 'anti-enforcement measure' for AI pacing?
o: Losses scale with a rule's expected lifespan, so actors push for weak rules, and hit at announcement
Investors shift their money toward labs in countries that refuse to join any pacing agreement at all
Stock exchanges are legally barred from listing any company covered by a pacing rule
Markets reward labs that publish safety research, which crowds out formal enforcement
ow: Their point is about durability and announcement effects, not where investors place money.
There is no such legal bar.
This is not the authors' argument.

units.title: Automated AI R&D
units.desc: IFP's plan for preparing for automated AI research (verification, state capacity, chip and weight security, the US lead), levers on AI R&D, and the 2026 pacing debate.

items.p: Why does IFP say AI verification technology matters for any future pacing of AI development?
o: Without it, deals need intrusive inspections; with it, targeted, checkable limits become possible
Verification would let the US government read the full contents of foreign labs' training data and weights
Verification is needed mainly because US domestic AI laws cannot be enforced without it
Verification would let AI companies skip safety evaluations, since compliance with any deal could be assumed
ow: IFP describes privacy-preserving methods designed so that sensitive information does not leave the facility.
IFP says domestic enforcement may be feasible today without new technology, relying on the threat of legal action.
IFP presents verification as a way to check that parties keep agreements; it says nothing about replacing evaluations.
keys: Without it, agreements need intrusive steps like mass inspections or data center shutdowns
Better verification allows targeted, checkable limits on the riskiest activities
Nuclear precedent: verification often needed before parties agree
items.x: IFP cites the nuclear arms control precedent: the ability to verify compliance is often necessary for parties to enter agreements at all. Without better verification, it warns, 'pacing' could become a euphemism for pausing.

items.p: IFP lists four kinds of AI compute verification technology. Match each to its description.
pairs: Data center metering
Devices record limited telemetry, like power draw, to infer what workload is running
Chip verification mechanisms
Secure features built into AI chips that verify privacy-preserving claims about their use
Spot checks on computation
Re-run a small sample of a counterparty's workloads to check they match expectations
AI inspectors
A trusted AI examines sensitive systems, reports only minimal findings, then wipes its memory
items.x: IFP says none of these is mature, with by some optimistic measures barely 50 people working on technical AI verification worldwide. It proposes an AI Verification Consortium (AIVEC) co-led by CAISI and industry, plus DARPA and NSF programs, to prototype and deploy them.

items.p: IFP proposes a verification 'grand challenge': teams run real AI workloads under mock agreements and win prizes for secretly breaking the agreements or for catching others who do. Why build in this adversarial element?
items.answer: Because any agreement that needs verification gives both sides strong incentives to cheat, including by tampering with the verification technology itself. Rewarding teams for evading and catching each other stress-tests the safeguards under realistic adversarial pressure and drives a race to the top.
keys: Real agreements give parties strong incentives to defect
Cheating can include tampering with the verification technology
Stress-tests safeguards under realistic adversarial pressure
items.x: IFP pairs this with simpler prizes paid to anyone who solves a well-specified problem, such as classifying workloads from data center telemetry. It cautions that a mock contest cannot match red-teaming by top nation-state actors, and wants the Intelligence Community to red-team its proposed pilot verifiable data center.

choice.p: Why does IFP want a verification competition that rewards teams for secretly breaking mock agreements?
o: Real deals tempt cheating, even tampering with verification tools, so they need adversarial stress tests
Prize money is the only legal way federal agencies can pay for verification research
Breaking mock agreements is mainly meant to train diplomats to negotiate and enforce real AI agreements
Competitions let labs keep their verification methods secret from government regulators
ow: IFP also backs grants and DARPA and NSF programs; prizes are one tool among several.
The contest is aimed at technical teams, not diplomats.
IFP wants verification that counterparties can trust, which secrecy would undercut.

items.p: IFP recommends that US intelligence agencies develop their own (unilateral) ways to monitor foreign AI compute. Give the two reasons IFP offers.
items.answer: Technical verification only works if parties are confident the other side has no large undeclared data centers. And deals to manage sudden AI R&D automation might be needed before verification technology is ready, so intelligence agencies would have to certify compliance.
keys: Confidence that the counterparty has no hidden data centers
Agreements may come before verification technology is ready
items.x: IFP compares this to how the Intelligence Community tracks fissile material to support International Atomic Energy Agency investigations, using signals and human intelligence, satellite and infrared imagery, and chip supply-chain intelligence.

choice.p: Why does IFP want US intelligence agencies to build unilateral ways to monitor foreign AI compute?
o: Verification fails if big data centers are hidden, and deals may come before verification is ready
Intelligence monitoring is far cheaper than verification technology, so it could replace that work entirely
Foreign labs have agreed to share their compute data only with US intelligence agencies, not with others
Unilateral monitoring would let the US enforce its own export controls inside China
ow: IFP presents intelligence monitoring as a complement to verification technology.
IFP describes no such agreement.
IFP's reasons concern verifying agreements, not enforcing US law abroad.

lessons.title: IFP's plan: state capacity, chips, weights and the lead

items.p: IFP argues that before any pacing of automated AI R&D, the US needs a trusted, well-resourced government AI body such as CAISI. Why does it say this is needed, and name one power it wants CAISI to have.
items.answer: IFP says only democratically accountable leadership can legitimately coordinate shifting resources toward defense and diffusion, and the US lacks institutions to track progress toward full automation, advise leaders and labs, and run that shift. Powers include: a direct line to a senior White House or cabinet official; staff placed inside frontier labs; organizing third-party evaluators.
keys: Only accountable leadership can legitimately coordinate a reallocation
US lacks institutions to track progress, advise and coordinate
One power: direct line to senior officials, staff inside labs, or organizing evaluators
items.x: IFP's Rec 3 calls a budget of at least 84 million dollars a year a minimum bar and says CAISI's autonomy and business model matter more than its size. It also wants CAISI to contract with labs on safety research and inform export controls, and says that without a state authority trusted across governments, parties, industry, media and the public, managing the pace would be impossible.

choice.p: Why does IFP say the US needs a trusted, well-resourced government AI body like CAISI before any pacing of automated AI R&D?
o: Only accountable leaders can legitimately shift resources, and the US lacks a body to steer it
Labs are legally barred from sharing safety information with each other, so government must hold it all
A government body could replace the labs' own internal safety teams and so cut the industry's overall costs
International law requires each country to name a single national AI regulator before it negotiates any deal
ow: IFP's case rests on legitimacy and capacity, not a ban on information sharing.
IFP wants CAISI to support labs' safety work, not replace it.
IFP cites no such international requirement.

items.p: IFP recommends extending the US AI lead over China. Name two ways IFP says a bigger lead would help manage the risks of automated AI R&D.
items.answer: Any two of: more time to build AI resilience; more leverage in international negotiations; easier to justify more risk management at home and abroad; room for US companies to shift compute from automated R&D to alignment, security and beneficial deployment.
keys: More time for resilience
More leverage in international negotiations
Easier to justify more risk management
Room to shift compute toward safety and deployment
items.x: In its Aug 2026 report, IFP estimated export controls give the US about a 10x compute advantage over China and roughly an 8-month capability lead. It says tighter chip and chipmaking-equipment controls, countering distillation (Chinese labs training on US model outputs) and preventing weight theft might extend the lead past 2 years in the best case.

choice.p: Which of these is a way IFP says a bigger US AI lead would help manage the risks of automated AI R&D?
o: It would give the US more leverage in international negotiations
It would let the US skip safety testing of its own frontier models
It would make cooperation with China unnecessary
It would let US labs automate AI research faster without oversight
ow: IFP says a secure lead would make more risk management easier to justify, not less.
IFP separately recommends preparing for cooperation with China, partly because the lead is small and fragile.
IFP says a lead would let companies shift compute away from automated R&D toward safety.

items.p: What does IFP want the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) to do with information about who buys US AI chips, and what two purposes would it serve?
items.answer: Ensure chipmakers keep visibility into their customers and gather this into an AI chip registry. It would help keep chips away from untrusted or irresponsible buyers, and support verification of agreements and intelligence collection.
keys: Chipmakers keep visibility into customers
BIS maintains an AI chip registry
Keeps chips from untrusted parties
Supports verification and intelligence work
items.x: IFP pairs this with tighter controls on chipmaking equipment, which it argues would ensure virtually all AI chips are produced by US chipmakers. It says the registry would support the verification and intelligence monitoring it recommends elsewhere in the report.

choice.p: What does IFP want BIS to do with information about who buys US AI chips?
o: Keep a BIS registry of buyers, tracked by chipmakers, to block untrusted buyers and aid verification
Publish every buyer's name online so that journalists and the public can track all US chip sales
Share the buyer lists with China as a confidence-building step before any AI talks
Use the buyer data to set and collect a new federal export tax on each advanced AI chip sold abroad
ow: IFP describes a registry held by BIS, not public disclosure.
IFP proposes no such sharing.
IFP's registry is for oversight, not taxation.

items.p: IFP calls for prototyping a highly secure (Security Level 4 or 5) AI cluster in a government facility. What two things is it meant to make possible?
items.answer: Moving highly sensitive model weights developed by industry into a much more secure facility if needed, to protect them from theft by nation-states; and evaluating future models, especially ones built through automated R&D, with less risk of them escaping containment.
keys: A secure place to move sensitive weights, safe from state-backed theft
Evaluate models with less risk of escape
items.x: IFP calls weights the 'crown jewels': distillation extracts only outputs, but theft hands over the whole model, and labs cannot currently stop well-resourced state actors. If a US model could fully automate AI R&D, IFP expects adversaries to prioritize stealing it. It cites RAND estimates of 37 to 50 million dollars for a proof-of-concept facility.

choice.p: What is IFP's proposed highly secure (SL4 or SL5) government AI cluster meant to make possible?
o: A secure place to move sensitive industry weights if needed, and to test new models with less risk of escape
A public cloud where any US researcher can train frontier models for free
A government lab that would replace private labs in building frontier models
A shared facility where US and Chinese labs could jointly train frontier models under international supervision
ow: This describes public compute proposals such as NAIRR, not IFP's secure cluster.
IFP's cluster is a fallback for industry weights, not a replacement for private labs.
IFP's cluster is meant to keep US weights away from adversaries.

items.p: While urging the US to extend its AI lead, IFP also wants to lay groundwork now for cooperating with China on automated AI R&D risks. Give the two reasons it offers.
items.answer: First, the US won't be the only relevant developer: its lead is only about 8 months and fragile given the risk of weight theft, and fast efficiency gains mean high-risk capabilities will eventually spread, so Chinese labs may face the same risks. Second, these risks cross borders, giving both countries an interest in dialogue.
keys: US lead is small and fragile; capabilities will diffuse
Chinese labs may face the same risks
Risks cross borders, so both sides gain from dialogue
items.x: IFP's Rec 22 wants the US-China AI dialogue to work on harmonized risk guidelines and on which verification technologies each side would use. It points to US-Soviet zero-trust verification in the Cold War as precedent for cooperating while competing.

choice.p: Why does IFP want to lay groundwork now for US-China cooperation on automated AI R&D risks, even while extending the US lead?
o: The US lead is small and fragile, the capabilities will spread, and the risks cross borders
China has already agreed to adopt US-style safety laws in exchange for renewed access to advanced US chips
Cooperation would let the US stop spending so much money on enforcing its advanced chip export controls
A treaty would let US labs move their largest data centers to China, where electric power is cheaper
ow: IFP describes no such agreement.
IFP wants tighter export controls alongside cooperation.
IFP proposes nothing of the kind.

lessons.title: R&D levers and the 2026 pacing debate

items.p: Match each AI R&D lever from the pacing.tech longlist to what it would measure or require.
pairs: Agent share of R&D compute
Fraction of a lab's R&D compute used by autonomous AI agents
R&D speed-up trigger
Safety-framework threshold tied to how much AI accelerates AI research
Human review ratio
Share of AI-written research code and experiment plans checked by humans
Safety case for the R&D stack
Structured safety argument required before deploying a model internally for R&D
Internal agent monitoring
How much of internal AI agents' activity is covered by monitoring
items.x: These levers appear in the pacing.tech longlist, which the authors present without endorsing. IFP asks companies to share related metrics, such as compute for AI-designed vs human-designed experiments and how often humans review delegated tasks.

items.p: Why do the pacing.tech authors say mandatory safety cases act as pacing interventions in regulated safety-critical industries?
items.answer: Work cannot proceed until the evidence is gathered into a safety case that would satisfy a regulator, and the work needed to build the case is aimed directly at the threats it covers.
keys: Work waits until a regulator-acceptable safety case exists
Building the case targets the relevant threats
items.x: The authors note that safety cases are not mandatory in frontier AI R&D and that few labs have produced them voluntarily. 'Safety case required before internal deployment on the R&D stack' appears in their longlist.

choice.p: Why do the pacing.tech authors say mandatory safety cases act as pacing interventions in regulated safety-critical industries?
o: Work waits on evidence a regulator would accept, and building it targets the threats
Safety cases impose a fixed waiting period of several years on every new engineering project
Safety cases require a local public vote before any large engineering or construction project begins
Safety cases raise firms' insurance costs so much that they cut back on their riskiest work
ow: The delay depends on gathering the evidence, not a fixed period.
Safety cases go to a regulator, not a public vote.
Their mechanism is the evidence requirement, not insurance costs.

items.p: In July 2026, over a thousand employees of frontier AI companies signed the 'Pacing the Frontier' statement. What single request did it make?
items.answer: That the US government support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.
keys: US government should support an international effort
To build technical and governance tools to pace automated AI development
items.x: The statement argues every company and country faces intense pressure not to slow down unilaterally, and that the world lacks tools to pace frontier-wide progress. It names no pause, threshold, or timeline. Its site listed 1,386 signers as of Oct 2026.

choice.p: What did the July 2026 'Pacing the Frontier' statement, signed by over a thousand frontier AI company employees, ask for?
o: US support for an international effort to build tools to pace automated AI development
An immediate six-month pause on training models above a compute threshold
A legal ban on AI labs using AI systems to automate their own research
That frontier labs stop selling access to their most capable models to foreign governments
ow: The statement names no pause, threshold or timeline; a six-month pause was the 2023 FLI letter's call.
It asks for tools to pace, not a ban.
It says nothing about foreign sales.

items.p: Dario Amodei's essay 'We Must Pace the Frontier' (Sept 2026) proposes a three-step plan. Name the three steps.
items.answer: 1) Embedded evaluators: third-party evaluators with employee-like access at each frontier AI company (Anthropic committed unilaterally). 2) Coordination among companies in democracies on safety standards and limits on the rate of progress, with government support such as an antitrust waiver. 3) Global coordination, including with authoritarian governments.
keys: Embedded third-party evaluators
Coordination among democracies' companies, with government support
Global coordination including authoritarian states
items.x: Amodei defines pacing as companies taking adequate time to align and safeguard their models, with third-party evaluators confirming this, and says it excludes halting model training or technical progress.

choice.p: Which of these is a step in Dario Amodei's three-step plan in 'We Must Pace the Frontier' (Sept 2026)?
o: Embedded third-party evaluators with employee-like access inside each frontier AI company
A federal government license required before any lab can begin any new frontier training run
A full global pause on all frontier AI development, starting in early 2027
Nationalizing the frontier labs and merging them into one US government AI project
ow: Amodei's plan does not include licensing.
He supports floating a full pause but expects it is unlikely soon; it is not one of his three steps.
His plan relies on company coordination with government support, not nationalization.

items.p: In 'We Must Pace the Frontier', what basis for pacing does Dario Amodei say he is most enthusiastic about, and what worry does he raise about limiting inputs like training compute?
items.answer: Pacing based on what a system can do and how safe it is observed to be, e.g. 'checkpoints': a model with capability X must come with certified alignment properties Y and Z. He worries input limits (compute, training runs, internal AI use to improve AI) may be more 'gameable'.
keys: Capability-based checkpoints requiring certified alignment properties
Input limits may be easier to game
items.x: His example: X might be 'able to escape or defeat most common sandboxing methods', with Y being whatever makes it very unlikely the model would break out and take over many computers.

choice.p: What basis for pacing is Dario Amodei most enthusiastic about, and what worry does he raise about limiting inputs like training compute?
o: Capability checkpoints requiring certified alignment properties; input limits may be easier to game
A fixed annual cap on training compute; capability tests are too slow to be run before each release
Limits on the number of staff at each lab; compute is too hard for outsiders to measure
Revenue caps on AI companies; capability limits would hurt US competitiveness abroad
ow: He worries input limits like compute caps may be more 'gameable'.
He proposes nothing about headcount.
He proposes no revenue caps.

items.p: Dario Amodei says pacing within democracies is limited by the US lead over China. Why, in his view, and name one measure he backs to protect that lead.
items.answer: If democracies slow by more than their lead, unpaced projects linked to the Chinese Communist Party pull ahead, bringing alignment risks and possible military dominance. Measures: no sales of powerful AI chips or chipmaking equipment to China, with crackdowns on smuggling and remote access; curbing unauthorized distillation; stronger lab security against weight theft.
keys: Slowing by more than the lead lets unpaced CCP-linked projects pull ahead
One measure: no powerful chips or chipmaking tools to China, curbing distillation, or preventing weight theft
items.x: He says these measures would widen the US lead over the next 3 to 5 years and argues they give democracies more leverage, making a later agreement with China more likely.

choice.p: Why does Dario Amodei say pacing within democracies is limited by the US lead over China?
o: Slowing by more than the lead would let unpaced CCP-linked projects pull ahead, with grave risks
US antitrust law forbids companies from coordinating to slow their work by more than their lead
China has promised to pause too if the US keeps its lead below an agreed size
Investors will only keep funding US labs that stay at least a year ahead of China
ow: Antitrust is a separate obstacle he raises for coordination among companies.
He describes no such promise.
He makes no claim about investor rules.

items.p: Dario Amodei floats a US-China 'speed limit' on recursive self-improvement (AI improving its own successors). Why does he think such a limit would cost each side little?
items.answer: Because slowing the rate of improvement from 'extremely fast' to 'only somewhat fast' gives up relatively little strategic advantage while potentially greatly improving safety.
keys: Slowing from extremely fast to only somewhat fast
Gives up little strategic advantage
Could greatly improve safety
items.x: He compares it to the SALT treaties, which capped missiles while preserving each country's deterrent, and calls such an agreement 'just on the edge of being possible'. His four levels run from bans on narrow dangerous uses like bioweapons, to mutual pre-release testing via a global standards body, to this speed limit, to a full pause he supports floating but expects is unlikely soon.

choice.p: Why does Dario Amodei think a US-China 'speed limit' on recursive self-improvement would cost each side little?
o: Slowing from extremely to somewhat fast costs little advantage but may greatly improve safety
Neither country's labs are yet capable of recursive self-improvement, so little would really be lost by limiting it
Both countries could keep secret models outside the agreement, so neither side really gives anything up
The limit would apply only to civilian models, leaving each country's military AI programs free to keep going
ow: He says self-improvement is already starting across the industry.
He treats secret models as a verification problem, not a reason the limit is cheap.
He does not describe a civilian-only limit.

items.p: In a September 2026 CNBC interview, Jay Clayton (Director of National Intelligence, named White House AI czar on Oct 4, 2026) rejected calls for an AI 'pause'. What reason did he give?
items.answer: Other countries around the world are continuing to develop AI, so he said he didn't think any American should consider a pause a good strategy.
keys: Other countries would keep developing AI
A pause is not a good strategy for the US
items.x: Responses differ. Dario Amodei accepts the concern and pairs pacing with tighter export controls to widen the US lead. Jeffrey Ding (ChinAI, Sept 2026) disputes the premise that US restraint would let China race ahead. In the same interview Clayton called superintelligence a 'national security issue'.

choice.p: What reason did Jay Clayton give in Sept 2026 for rejecting calls for an AI pause?
o: Other countries keep developing AI, so he doesn't think a US pause is a good strategy
AI is not yet capable enough to pose any serious national security risk
A pause would violate AI developers' First Amendment rights
Only Congress, not the White House, has the legal authority to approve a pause
ow: He called superintelligence a 'national security issue', so he did not dismiss its risks.
He made a competition argument, not a constitutional one.
His stated reason was international competition.

items.p: Dario Amodei proposes embedded third-party evaluators (such as METR) inside AI companies, citing bank supervisors as precedent. Name two objections Dave Karpf raises in Tech Policy Press (Sept 2026).
items.answer: Any two of: bank supervisors exist only because government requires them, and without enforcement monitors get captured (as with Arthur Andersen and Enron); lower-paid evaluators would drift toward lab jobs; the small AI safety community is socially entangled with the labs; industry should not design its own regulation.
keys: Without government force, embedded monitors get captured
Pay gap pulls evaluators toward lab jobs
AI safety community is too entangled with labs
Industry shouldn't write its own rules
items.x: Karpf's alternative: an enforced regulatory system with clear liability and punitive damages (e.g. if a model escapes its sandbox and hacks websites), plus transparency regimes the industry does not pick for itself. Amodei calls embedded evaluators the key step for verifying any pacing commitments and says labs should partner with government to formalize them.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection Dave Karpf raises to Dario Amodei's embedded-evaluator proposal?
o: Without enforcement, embedded monitors get captured, as Arthur Andersen was by Enron
Embedded evaluators would leak the lab's trade secrets and model details to rival Chinese labs
Evaluators would slow AI progress so much that the US would end up losing its lead to China
Banks have never actually used embedded supervisors, so the banking precedent is invented
ow: Karpf's concern is capture, not leaks to China.
Karpf wants more regulatory friction, not less.
Karpf accepts the banking precedent but notes the supervisors exist because government requires them.

items.p: Jeffrey Ding (ChinAI newsletter, Sept 2026) critiqued Dario Amodei's claim that if US labs slow down, China will race ahead. What logical tension does Ding point to?
items.answer: Amodei also says Chinese labs catch up largely through distillation and model weight theft. If that is true, a US slowdown would also slow Chinese progress, since they would be copying weaker models at a slower rate.
keys: Amodei says China catches up via distillation and weight theft
Then a US slowdown would slow China too
items.x: Ding also defines AI leadership as a long 'diffusion marathon' of adopting a general-purpose technology across the economy, and argues that on this view withholding powerful AI chips from China would be counterproductive. He favors lower-level US-China cooperation, such as lab-to-lab technical exchanges and international industry safety associations, over a leaders' grand bargain.

choice.p: What logical tension does Jeffrey Ding (ChinAI, Sept 2026) see in Dario Amodei's claim that China would race ahead if US labs slowed down?
o: Amodei says China catches up via distillation and theft, so a US slowdown would slow China too
Amodei says China has no real frontier labs of its own, yet warns that Chinese labs could overtake the US
Amodei supports selling powerful chips to China while warning loudly about the dangers of Chinese AI
Amodei says pacing should be global while refusing any talks with China
ow: Amodei does not claim China lacks frontier labs.
Amodei opposes selling powerful AI chips to China.
Amodei's plan includes attempting global coordination with China.

items.p: Which of these positions comes from IFP's Aug 2026 report on automated AI R&D?
o: Adopt low-regret steps now (transparency, state capacity, verification, resilience) so targeted pacing is possible later
Frontier labs should host embedded evaluators and coordinate under a narrow antitrust waiver, with Anthropic committing to the first step now
Government should enforce clear liability with punitive damages, plus transparency rules, instead of letting the AI industry shape its own regulation
AI leadership is a decades-long diffusion marathon, so withholding powerful AI chips from China would be counterproductive
ow: This is Dario Amodei's plan in 'We Must Pace the Frontier'.
This is Dave Karpf's alternative in Tech Policy Press (Sept 2026).
This is Jeffrey Ding's argument in ChinAI #375 (Sept 2026).
keys: Low-regret measures now: transparency, state capacity, verification, resilience
Prepare so targeted pacing is possible if risks materialize
items.x: IFP frames its 23 recommendations as preparation: building information, capacity, and technology so that a targeted response is available if automated AI R&D proves dangerous.

units.title: Transparency and reporting
units.desc: Policies that make frontier AI labs disclose plans, test results, incidents, internal model use and compute, and the main arguments for and against each.

items.p: California, New York and Illinois have passed laws requiring large frontier AI developers to publish a 'frontier AI framework'. Name two things such a framework has to describe.
items.answer: Any two of: which dangerous capabilities the developer tests for (such as bioweapons help, offensive cyber, loss of control); what thresholds trigger extra safeguards; how it secures model weights; who inside the company makes the decisions.
keys: Which dangerous capabilities are tested for
Thresholds that trigger extra safeguards
How model weights are secured
Who inside the company decides
items.x: This is the design of California's SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act), copied by New York's RAISE Act and Illinois SB 315. The law sets no safety standard of its own; it requires the lab to write down and publish its own.

choice.p: Which of these must a 'frontier AI framework' describe under California's SB 53 and similar state laws?
o: What capability thresholds would trigger extra safeguards
The full training dataset used for each of its frontier models
The salaries of the company's safety staff
A list of every customer using the model
ow: Training-data disclosure is a separate California law (AB 2013), not part of the framework.
Frameworks cover risk governance, not pay.
Frameworks do not list customers.

items.p: California's SB 53 (in force since January 2026) requires large frontier developers to publish and follow a safety framework. Which developers does it cover?
items.answer: Developers with more than 500 million dollars in annual revenue that train models using more than 10^26 operations (a training compute threshold).
keys: Revenue above 500 million dollars
Training compute above 10^26 operations
items.x: The California Attorney General enforces SB 53, with penalties of up to 1 million dollars per violation. New York and Illinois copied the design, with effect from 2027.

choice.p: Which developers does California's SB 53 require to publish and follow a safety framework?
o: Over 500 million dollars in annual revenue, training models with more than 10^26 operations
Any company of any size that offers an AI chatbot to California residents
Any developer training a model with more than 10^25 operations, whatever its revenue
Only developers that release open-weight models used by over 1 million people
ow: SB 53 targets large frontier developers, not every chatbot provider.
10^25 is the EU AI Act's systemic-risk threshold; SB 53 uses 10^26 plus a revenue test for these duties.
SB 53 covers large frontier developers whether or not they release weights.

items.p: Safety framework laws like SB 53 set no safety standard of their own. How do supporters say they still reduce catastrophic risk?
items.answer: Labs otherwise set safety rules privately and can quietly loosen them under competitive pressure. Publishing creates a public baseline that journalists, watchdogs, employees and regulators can check releases against, and a duty to follow the framework turns broken promises into legal violations.
keys: Counters quiet loosening under competitive pressure
Public baseline outsiders can check releases against
Duty to follow makes broken promises legal violations
items.x: Supporters also call it a low-cost first step that builds information for later rules. The argument assumes frameworks are specific enough to be violated and that someone (an attorney general, regulator or auditor) actually enforces them.

choice.p: Safety framework laws set no safety standard of their own. How do supporters say they still reduce risk?
o: Outsiders can check releases against the published plan, and breaking it is illegal
The state reviews each framework in detail and rejects any that are too weak to keep the public safe
Labs must buy liability insurance sized to the catastrophic risks that their frameworks describe
Frameworks give the state power to shut down any model that it considers too dangerous to release
ow: Under SB 53 the lab writes its own framework; state minimum standards are a separate, stronger variant.
Insurance mandates are a different policy tool.
Shutdown authority is a different tool (emergency powers).

items.p: Safety framework rules can take a 'publish only' or a 'publish and follow' form. What is the difference?
o: Publish and follow makes the lab legally bound to comply with its framework; publish only requires the document
Publish only requires the framework to be filed with a regulator, while publish and follow requires a public website version
Publish and follow requires a government agency to write the framework, while publish only lets the lab write it
Publish only applies to open-weight models, while publish and follow applies to closed models only
ow: Filing with a regulator is a separate variant; it is not what distinguishes these two.
In both versions the lab writes its own framework; minimum content standards set by the state are a separate variant.
Neither version is defined by open versus closed weights.
keys: Publish and follow: legally bound to comply with its own framework
Deviations become enforceable
Publish only: the document just has to exist
items.x: Publish only resembles the earlier voluntary Seoul Frontier AI Safety Commitments. Publish and follow is the model used by California SB 53, New York's RAISE Act, Illinois SB 315 and the federal FRONTIER Act bill.

items.p: Laws like California SB 53 require frontier labs to publish and follow their own safety framework. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: the law is light-touch because labs choose their own rules (The Midas Project); frameworks are vague and score low, median 18 percent across 12 companies (SaferAI); labs have weakened or voided pause pledges (FLI AI Safety Index); vague duties are hard to comply with (Council for Citizens Against Government Waste); barriers to entry for small developers (industry letter on RAISE).
keys: Light-touch: labs choose their own rules (Midas Project)
Frameworks are vague and score poorly (SaferAI)
Labs weaken their own pause pledges (FLI)
Too vague to comply with (CCAGW, Tennessee bill)
Barriers to entry for smaller developers (RAISE industry letter)
items.x: In September 2026 the Midas Project alleged that OpenAI's Astra releases may have violated SB 53; OpenAI said it was confident it complied. Supporters' reply to the vagueness problem is stronger variants: minimum content standards set by the state, or third-party review of compliance.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to laws requiring labs to publish and follow their own safety frameworks?
o: Labs write their own rules, so a vague framework is hard to violate
The laws force labs to publish their model weights
The laws let the state block any model release it dislikes
The laws set a single federal standard that overrides every state's own rules
ow: Framework laws require a written risk plan, not weight release.
SB 53 gives the state no power to approve or block releases.
SB 53 is a state law; federal preemption is a separate debate.

items.p: Model and system card mandates require developers to publish documentation of each new frontier model. Under frontier-focused versions, name two things the disclosure must cover.
items.answer: Any two of: results of dangerous-capability evaluations (chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear weapons uplift, offensive cyber, autonomous loss of control); the safeguards applied; whether outside testers were involved; how the model was tested.
keys: Dangerous-capability evaluation results (CBRN, cyber, loss of control)
Safeguards applied
Whether outside testers were involved
How the model was tested
items.x: California SB 53 requires a transparency report at release. The federal AI Systems Transparency Act (S. 5471) would have the Federal Trade Commission require model cards, including an affirmative statement for any risk domain (such as CBRN, cyber or loss of control) where no evaluation was done.

choice.p: Which of these must frontier-focused model card mandates make developers disclose?
o: Results of dangerous-capability evaluations, such as bioweapons uplift and offensive cyber
The model's full weights, so that outside researchers can download and retest it themselves
The names and roles of every employee who worked on building the model
The revenue the company expects the model to earn over its first year
ow: Model cards describe testing and safeguards; they don't release weights.
Model cards don't list staff.
Revenue projections are not part of model cards.

items.p: AI labs already publish model or system cards voluntarily. Why do supporters want disclosure to be mandatory and standardized?
items.answer: Voluntary timing and content are inconsistent: Google released Gemini 2.5 Pro in March 2025 without a safety report. Mandatory, standard disclosure lets researchers, deployers and governments compare models, spot dangerous capability jumps and check that claimed safeguards exist, and builds a record that liability and enforcement can use.
keys: Voluntary timing and content are inconsistent (e.g. Gemini 2.5 Pro)
Lets outsiders compare models and spot capability jumps
Check claimed safeguards; record for liability and enforcement
items.x: A short Gemini 2.5 Pro model card followed about three weeks after release, and 60 UK parliamentarians called the delay a breach of Google's Seoul safety commitments; Google DeepMind said it was meeting its public commitments. Supporters assume disclosed evaluations are honest and that disclosure does not itself leak hazardous details.

choice.p: Labs already publish model cards voluntarily. Why do supporters want disclosure to be mandatory and standardized?
o: Voluntary cards vary in timing and content; standard ones let outsiders compare models
Voluntary model cards break trade secret law unless a statute requires them
Mandatory cards would let the government approve each model before release
Standard cards would remove the need for labs to run their own dangerous-capability tests at all
ow: Labs publish voluntary cards legally today.
Disclosure mandates require documentation, not pre-approval.
Model cards report test results; they don't replace testing.

items.p: A law would require AI developers to publish model cards with dangerous-capability test results at release. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: compelled disclosure is speech regulation and may fail First Amendment review, especially when it requires judgments rather than facts (Sokhansanj and Arnold, Lawfare; xAI's suit against a California disclosure law); self-reported evaluations miss flaws outsiders find (Longpre et al.); detailed results can spread hazardous information (the reason the EU allows redacted summaries).
keys: First Amendment risk (Sokhansanj and Arnold; xAI lawsuit)
Self-reported tests give limited assurance (Longpre et al.)
Detailed results can leak hazardous information
items.x: Under the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, the full safety report goes to the EU AI Office and the public version can be redacted. Longpre et al. propose protected third-party flaw disclosure to address the self-reporting problem.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to requiring model cards with dangerous-capability test results?
o: Detailed results can spread hazardous information
Model cards would reveal users' private chat histories to the public
Disclosure would let the FTC block new model releases at will
Model cards are far too short to be useful to anyone reading them
ow: Model cards describe the model, not users' chats.
Disclosure mandates require publication, not FTC approval.
Critics focus on legal risk, self-reporting and hazards, not length.

items.p: Match each model-disclosure variant to the proposal or law that uses it.
pairs: FTC-enforced consumer and safety model cards
AI Systems Transparency Act (Coons, Britt, Schatz, Lankford)
Full report to a regulator, redacted public summary
EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice
Model access a fixed time before release
Warner's AI Risk Management and Security Act (45-day access)
Protected reporting of flaws by outside researchers
Proposed by Longpre et al.
items.x: Consumer-protection model cards cover more models but go shallower on catastrophic risk, while confidential reports to a regulator reduce trade-secret and hazard concerns.

items.p: Under California SB 53 and similar state laws, what kinds of events count as a 'critical safety incident' that must be reported? Name two.
items.answer: Any two of: unauthorized access to or theft of model weights that causes death or injury; harm from a catastrophic risk materializing; loss of control of a model that causes death or injury; a model using deceptive techniques to evade its developer's controls in a way that shows materially increased catastrophic risk.
keys: Theft of or unauthorized access to model weights (causing harm)
Harm from a catastrophic risk
Loss of control of a model (causing harm)
Model deceptively evading developer controls
items.x: Critics such as Arnold and Llerena (LawAI) note that three of the four categories require actual harm. Under SB 53, reports go to the Office of Emergency Services confidentially, and anonymized annual summaries start in 2027.

choice.p: Which of these counts as a 'critical safety incident' under California SB 53?
o: A model deceptively evading its developer's controls in a way that shows higher catastrophic risk
A chatbot giving a user incorrect medical advice that delays their treatment for a serious illness
A data breach that exposes customers' names and email addresses to hackers
A new model scoring much higher than expected on a public coding benchmark
ow: SB 53's categories concern catastrophic risk, not ordinary product errors.
Customer data breaches fall under other laws.
A benchmark result is not an incident under SB 53.

items.p: Match each regime to its AI incident reporting deadline.
pairs: California SB 53
15 days to the Office of Emergency Services; 24 hours to an appropriate authority if death or serious injury is imminent
New York RAISE Act and Illinois SB 315
72 hours
EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice
2 to 15 days depending on incident type
AI Kill Switch Act (House bill)
15-day reports to the Department of Homeland Security
items.x: The pacing.tech appendix lists an 'incident reporting deadline' as one transparency intervention, citing SB 53. As of Oct 2026 the AI Kill Switch Act (H.R. 9917, Reps. Lieu and Moran) has not passed; it was referred to committee in July 2026. The New York and Illinois deadlines apply from 2027.

items.p: How do supporters say mandatory AI incident reporting to government would help? Name two ways.
items.answer: Any two of: early warning of dangerous behavior (governments now learn of failures from the press or victims); a dataset of near misses across companies; a trigger for emergency response, as in aviation and cybersecurity incident regimes.
keys: Early warning of dangerous behavior
