A released model can never be recalled once its weights are out
Open models are always too weak to pose any serious danger
ow: That is an argument for limits, drawn from FAR.AI's research.
That is an argument for limits: once weights are out, safeguards can't be added back.
Opponents say the extra risk is unproven; they don't claim open models can never be dangerous.

items.p: Mandatory DNA synthesis screening would require companies that make synthetic DNA to check orders and customers. How do supporters say it reduces AI-enabled bioweapon risk?
items.answer: AI may lower the knowledge barrier to designing pathogens, but a design still needs physical DNA. Synthesis is a narrow industry, so screening there is a chokepoint that works no matter which AI model was used, including open-weight ones.
keys: Designs still need physical DNA to become weapons
Synthesis is a concentrated chokepoint
Works regardless of the AI model, including open-weight
items.x: The Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act (S. 3741, Cotton-Klobuchar) would require all providers, including makers of benchtop synthesizers, to screen orders and customers and keep records. As of October 2026 it sits in Senate Commerce, with a House companion (H.R. 10197) introduced August 31, 2026. Today's federal framework binds only federally funded researchers.

choice.p: How do supporters say mandatory DNA synthesis screening reduces AI-enabled bioweapon risk?
o: Designs still need physical DNA from a narrow industry, whichever AI model was used
Screening lets regulators see which AI models people have asked about dangerous pathogens
Screening stops AI labs from training their models on published biology research papers
Screening forces developers of open-weight models to build in safety filters before release
ow: Screening checks DNA orders and customers; it gives no view into how people use AI models.
Filtering training data is a separate proposal that acts on the model.
Screening acts on the physical DNA step and puts no requirement on models.

items.p: Mandatory DNA synthesis screening checks orders against lists of dangerous sequences. Name two problems or gaps researchers and officials have raised.
items.answer: Examples: AI protein-design tools made variants that evaded several screening systems until patched, so sequence matching may fall behind (Wittmann, Horvitz et al., Science, Oct 2025); federal action has stalled, with no revised framework 400+ days after one was ordered (Sen. Ossoff, June 2026); benchtop synthesizers and foreign providers may escape screening.
keys: AI-designed variants evaded sequence screens (Science 2025)
Federal revision stalled (Ossoff letter, June 2026)
Benchtop synthesizers or foreign providers may escape screening
items.x: These critiques push for stronger screening: 'AI-resilient' screening that detects functional variants instead of relying on sequence similarity alone, coverage of benchtop machines, and adoption by other countries. OSTP had been ordered in May 2025 to revise the screening framework within 90 days.

choice.p: Which is a problem researchers have raised with DNA synthesis screening?
o: AI-designed protein variants evaded several screening systems until they were patched
Screening requires providers to publish every customer's name online
Screening has been mandatory for all US providers since 2020, yet orders still slip through
Screening bans most legitimate research on pathogens
ow: Screening involves vetting customers, but no proposal requires publishing their names.
Screening is still voluntary for most providers; only federally funded buyers face a requirement.
Screening checks orders and customers; it does not ban research.

units.title: Power, government and international
units.desc: Who controls advanced AI: military AI, coup-proofing government AI, market structure, public compute, federal preemption, and international agreements.

items.p: Most limits on US military AI sit in internal Defense Department policy, such as Directive 3000.09 on autonomous weapons. What failure do supporters of statutory limits want to prevent, and why do they want the limits in law?
items.answer: A military that uses lethal force or watches its own citizens at machine speed with few humans in the loop, so fewer people can refuse an illegal or catastrophic order. That risks accidents (such as an AI-triggered nuclear exchange) and misuse by a small group. A statute is harder for one Secretary or President to change than a directive.
keys: Force or surveillance at machine speed with few humans
Fewer people able to refuse illegal orders
Accidents (nuclear) and misuse by a small group
Statute is harder to waive or change than internal policy
items.x: Supporters would ideally extend similar limits to DHS, the FBI and intelligence agencies. The approach assumes limits are drafted without broad exceptions and that Congress can see whether DoD complies.

choice.p: Why do supporters want limits on military AI written into statute instead of DoD policy?
o: One Secretary or President can change internal policy; a statute is harder to waive
Courts cannot review any military decision unless Congress first passes a statute on it
A US statute would automatically bind other countries' militaries
DoD has no written policy on autonomous weapons at all
ow: The case for statute is durability against executive change; court review is a separate question.
A US statute binds only the US government.
DoD does have a policy, Directive 3000.09; supporters want something harder to change.

items.p: What is the legal force of Sec. 1638 of the FY2025 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) on AI and nuclear weapons?
o: A non-binding policy statement that nuclear use needs positive human action
A binding ban on using AI in any US weapons system, nuclear or conventional
An executive order requiring a human decision before any US nuclear launch
A US-China treaty commitment to keep humans in control of nuclear launch
ow: It covers nuclear use only and is not binding; binding versions appear in the FY27 Senate text.
It is a provision in a statute passed by Congress, not an executive order.
No US-China treaty on AI and nuclear launch exists.
items.x: The FY2027 Senate defense bill (S. 4784) would make a nuclear human-control rule binding and add a domestic surveillance limit. It failed a cloture vote 50-46 in July 2026 and had not passed the Senate as of mid-October 2026; the House-passed version lacks these limits.
keys: Non-binding sense of Congress
Statement of policy that nuclear use needs positive human action

items.p: Match each military AI proposal to its description.
pairs: Nuclear human-control rule
Bars AI from the decision to launch or detonate a nuclear weapon
Slotkin AI Guardrails Act
Bars DoD from using AI to monitor or target people in the US without legal basis
Gillibrand autonomous weapons ban
General ban with exceptions for supervised, defensive or non-lethal systems
Process controls
Senior sign-off, testing, logging and audit for high-consequence uses
Distributed control (Forethought)
No single person can command enough autonomous force to stage a coup
items.x: Process controls appear in Sen. Gillibrand's Secure and Accountable Military AI Act of 2026 (S. 4656), which also contains the autonomous weapons ban; they create records Congress can inspect. S. 4656 had no cosponsors as of October 2026. Forethought's distributed-control idea is not yet in bill text.

items.p: Sen. Slotkin's AI Guardrails Act would bar the Pentagon from using autonomous weapons to kill 'without appropriate levels of human judgment and supervision.' Name two objections critics have raised to military AI limits like this.
items.answer: Examples: Roberto González called the undefined word 'appropriate' a loophole likely to make the law meaningless; John Ramming Chappell (Center for Civilians in Conflict) says Congress should have to vote to allow a system instead of leaving it to presidential waivers; the AI Now Institute says military AI lacks basic safety assurance and backs a moratorium on military uses until it exists.
keys: 'Appropriate' is undefined, a loophole (González)
Waivers give the executive free rein; Congress should vote (Chappell)
Military AI lacks safety assurance; AI Now backs a moratorium
items.x: González and Chappell were quoted in Responsible Statecraft. Slotkin's bill lets the defense secretary waive the limit in 'extraordinary circumstances', while Gillibrand's bill requires a joint resolution of Congress for fully autonomous systems. From the other direction, Pentagon technology chief Emil Michael pushed AI vendors to accept 'all lawful use' of their models and criticized Anthropic's refusal to allow fully autonomous weapons use.

choice.p: Which objection have critics raised to the 'appropriate levels of human judgment' standard in Sen. Slotkin's AI Guardrails Act?
o: 'Appropriate' is undefined, a loophole that could make the law meaningless
It requires a joint resolution of Congress before any AI system is used
It would hand control of military AI decisions to private AI companies
It covers only nuclear weapons, leaving drones unregulated
ow: Gillibrand's bill has a joint-resolution requirement for fully autonomous systems, an approach Chappell says is preferable to waivers.
The bill limits DoD's own use; vendor terms were a separate Pentagon-Anthropic dispute.
The standard covers autonomous weapons used to kill; nuclear launch is a separate rule.

lessons.title: Coup-proofing and government use of AI

items.p: What is 'law-following AI' (LFAI), and how do supporters at the Institute for Law & AI say it would guard against power grabs?
items.answer: AI agents built to refuse clearly illegal actions, even when government officials order them. Coups and executive power grabs have needed many people to cooperate, some of whom refuse. If AI replaces soldiers and civil servants, LFAI keeps that refusal capacity inside the system.
keys: AI agents refuse clearly unlawful orders, including from officials
Power grabs historically needed many cooperating people
LFAI preserves the check that human refusal provided
Cheapest route: procurement requirements
items.x: Cullen O'Keefe and colleagues at LawAI propose requiring LFAI, for example through procurement terms, for AI agents in high-stakes government roles. As of Oct 2026 no bill requires it.

choice.p: How do supporters say law-following AI, built to refuse clearly illegal orders even from officials, would guard against power grabs?
o: Power grabs need many people's help; AI that refuses illegal orders preserves that check
It lets federal courts switch off any government AI system found to have broken a law
It requires Congress to approve each sensitive government AI deployment in advance by statute
It audits government models for hidden loyalties that insiders inserted during training
ow: Law-following AI works through the model's own refusals; it gives courts no off switch.
Advance congressional approval is O'Keefe's separate 'advice and consent' proposal.
Secret-loyalty audits are Forethought's related but separate proposal.

items.p: Law-following AI: government AI agents must refuse clearly unlawful orders. What objections have been raised? Name two.
items.answer: Examples: Cullen O'Keefe (LawAI) notes laws have gaps that clever AIs will find, and law-following AI cannot stop legal but harmful loophole use; Katalina Hernandez Delgado argues that following the law's letter invites gaming, while following its spirit collapses back into value alignment; DoD's demand that vendors accept 'all lawful use' cuts against model-level refusals.
keys: Laws have gaps; LFAI can't stop legal loophole use (O'Keefe)
Letter of the law invites gaming; its spirit needs value judgments (Hernandez Delgado)
DoD wants 'all lawful use' without vendor limits
items.x: O'Keefe's own answer to the gaps problem (Lawfare, May 2026) is congressional 'advice and consent': AI in protected uses, which he says might include criminal investigations, domestic intelligence, domestic military deployment and prosecutions, would be barred unless Congress authorizes it by statute.

choice.p: Which is an objection raised to law-following AI requirements for government AI agents?
o: Laws have gaps, so an AI can help abuse power while staying legal
It forces every AI user to reveal their identity, at a cost to privacy
It builds a remote off switch into AI chips that hackers could exploit
It amounts to a large subsidy for the biggest cloud companies
ow: That is an objection to AI agent identification schemes.
That is an objection to remote-disable features in chips.
That is an objection to public compute built on commercial clouds.

items.p: Forethought researchers (Davidson, Finnveden and Hadshar) propose 'secret-loyalty audits' and distributed control of powerful AI. What risk are these meant to address?
items.answer: That a lab insider or a single official quietly gains control over powerful AI, for example by training hidden instructions into a model so it serves one person or faction, and then uses it to seize power.
keys: AI-enabled coups by a small group
Audits check models for hidden objectives
No single person can direct enough AI capability alone
Coup-proof any single centralized AI project
items.x: Distributed control means, for example, that no single person can control enough military AI systems to stage a coup. The Forethought report (April 2025) also says any plan for a single centralized AI project should be coup-proofed.

choice.p: What risk are Forethought's proposed 'secret-loyalty audits' and distributed control of powerful AI meant to address?
o: An insider or single official secretly controlling powerful AI to seize power
Rival countries stealing frontier model weights through large-scale cyberattacks
AI models deceiving their own developers by hiding capabilities during safety testing
Chinese firms renting export-controlled US chips through cloud data centers abroad
ow: Weight theft by states is the target of security standards; these tools target insiders and small groups.
Deception during testing is a loss-of-control concern with its own detection tools.
Cloud rental is an export-control gap, handled by know-your-customer rules.

items.p: Limits on government use of AI against the public cover surveillance, policing and immigration enforcement. How do supporters say such limits help?
items.answer: AI lowers the cost of watching, sorting and acting against many people, letting a government do at scale what once needed thousands of cooperating staff. Bans and approval rules restore friction for the riskiest uses, and logging and audits let courts, Congress and the press see misuse.
keys: AI removes the need for many cooperating staff
Bans/approvals add friction to the riskiest uses
Logging and audits make misuse visible
items.x: Tools range from bans (the ICE Out of Our Faces Act would bar ICE and CBP facial recognition) to process rules in OMB memo M-25-21 (impact assessments, human review, appeals) to oversight such as logging government AI use and expanding GAO audits. As of Oct 2026 the bans have no Republican sponsors.

choice.p: How do supporters say limits on government use of AI against the public help?
o: AI replaces the many staff abuse once needed; limits add friction and logs expose it
They stop federal agencies from buying AI models built by Chinese companies
They make agencies buy from several AI vendors so no single firm gets locked in
They protect agencies' own AI systems from being hacked by foreign intelligence services
ow: Country-of-origin limits are a separate, security-focused proposal.
Multi-vendor rules are a market-structure and procurement tool.
Protecting government systems is a separate concern; these limits restrain the government itself.

items.p: Limits on government use of AI against the public include proposed bans on immigration agencies using facial recognition. Name one objection or obstacle that has been raised.
items.answer: Examples: a DHS spokesperson said banning ICE and CBP facial recognition would limit tracking criminals and make communities less safe; legal scholar Ashley Deeks argues national security AI is a 'double black box' (government secrecy plus model opacity), so limits are hard to enforce without new inspection tools; vague exceptions leave the executive to define the limit.
keys: DHS: bans weaken law enforcement and public safety
Deeks: secrecy plus model opacity block oversight
Vague exceptions leave the executive to define the limit
items.x: Drafting matters: the Senate defense bill's committee text bars only DoD surveillance 'not otherwise permissible' under the Constitution, a looser standard than the individualized legal basis in Sen. Slotkin's standalone bill. As of October 2026 the facial recognition bans have no Republican sponsors.

choice.p: Which is an objection or obstacle raised to limits on government use of AI against the public?
o: Government secrecy plus model opacity make the limits hard to enforce
The limits would force agencies to publish the source code of their AI systems
The limits would apply to private companies instead of government
Facial recognition is already banned at every federal agency, so the bills are moot
ow: The proposals restrict uses and add oversight; none requires publishing source code.
These limits target government agencies specifically.
No federal ban exists; the bills to ban it for ICE and CBP have not left committee.

items.p: Antitrust and market-structure remedies aim to stop a few firms controlling the AI stack. Match each remedy to its description.
pairs: Partnership and merger review
Scrutinize lab-cloud investments and exclusive deals as mergers
Structural separation
Bar firms that own chips or cloud from also owning leading models
Multi-vendor procurement
Require government buyers, such as DoD, to use several AI vendors
Supervised pacing body
Government-supervised standards body to pace the frontier, instead of an antitrust exemption
items.x: The FTC studied cloud-lab partnerships (Microsoft-OpenAI, Amazon-Anthropic, Google-Anthropic) under its 6(b) authority but took no enforcement action. Structural separation comes from Narechania and Sitaraman (2024); the supervised body from Open Markets (Oct 2026). Multi-vendor language is in the Senate FY27 defense bill (S. 4784), which had not passed the Senate as of mid-October 2026.

items.p: Antitrust remedies for frontier AI would use merger review and structural separation against concentration. Name one objection or complication that has been raised.
items.answer: Examples: FTC Commissioner Melissa Holyoak (June 2025) said enforcers should not set AI market structure in advance, since imposing views on how many competitors there should be would dampen innovation and help foreign firms; Mark MacCarthy (Brookings) argues a growing problem is labs competing with customers who depend on their models, which antitrust law is unlikely to address.
keys: Holyoak (FTC): enforcers shouldn't set market structure in advance; it dampens innovation
MacCarthy: labs competing with dependent customers, which antitrust handles poorly
items.x: Holyoak spoke in a personal capacity in a June 2025 speech, in which she also said competition among foundation-model developers was intense for now but the market would likely consolidate. The FTC's study of cloud-lab partnerships produced a report but no enforcement, and the current FTC leadership has signaled less appetite for action.

choice.p: Which is an objection raised to antitrust remedies against concentration in frontier AI?
o: Setting AI market structure in advance would dampen innovation
Merger review would force frontier labs to publish their model weights openly
Existing antitrust law already bars AI labs from owning their own cloud servers
The EU AI Act already requires chip, cloud and model firms to be separate companies
ow: Merger review examines deals and ownership; it has nothing to do with publishing weights.
No US law bars labs from owning cloud infrastructure; separation is only a proposal.
The EU AI Act regulates model risks; it does not split up the AI stack.

items.p: What is the National AI Research Resource (NAIRR), and what would the CREATE AI Act do?
items.answer: NAIRR gives academic and nonprofit researchers subsidized compute and data, run as a National Science Foundation pilot. The CREATE AI Act would make it permanent; as of Oct 2026 the Senate version (S. 4441, April 2026) sits in committee.
keys: Subsidized compute and data for researchers
Runs as an NSF pilot
CREATE AI Act would make it permanent
items.x: Supporters say public compute lets academics and public-interest groups study frontier systems and check industry claims. California's SB 53 also created CalCompute, a planned public cloud cluster, contingent on funding. Current public resources are tiny next to private frontier clusters.

o: An NSF pilot offering researchers subsidized compute; CREATE AI makes it permanent
A Commerce program that tests frontier models for risks; CREATE AI would fund it
A federal registry of AI chips; CREATE AI would require chipmakers to report every sale
A public cloud cluster run by California; CREATE AI would expand it nationwide
ow: Government model testing is the job of CAISI at NIST.
A chip registry is an export-control proposal from IFP and others.
California's public cloud plan is CalCompute, created by SB 53.

items.p: Public compute and public AI projects range from research clouds to an international AGI project. What objections have been raised? Name one.
items.answer: Examples: AI Now and Data & Society (Meredith Whittaker, 2021) argued a resource built on licensed commercial cloud is a subsidy to Big Tech; Forethought researchers warn a centralized government or multinational AI project concentrates control in a few officials unless it is coup-proofed.
keys: Subsidizes the largest cloud firms (AI Now, Data & Society)
Centralized projects concentrate power (Forethought)
Forethought: coup-proof centralized projects (oversight by several bodies, use rules)
items.x: Forethought's AI-enabled coups report (Davidson, Finnveden and Hadshar, April 2025) says any plan for a single centralized AI project should be coup-proofed, for example with oversight by several government bodies, including legislative committees and courts, and formal rules on how its AI may be used.

choice.p: Which is an objection raised to public compute and public AI projects?
o: Built on licensed commercial cloud, it would mainly subsidize Big Tech
It would let Chinese researchers use US public research compute for free
It would require universities to stop using private cloud providers for research
It would ban private companies from training frontier models outside the public system
ow: NAIRR serves US researchers; foreign access is not the objection raised.
Public compute adds an option; it bars no one from private clouds.
Public compute supplements private development; it bans nothing.

items.p: Match each preemption approach to its description.
pairs: Blanket moratorium
Bars most state AI laws for years with no federal standard
Executive preemption campaign
Lawsuits and grant conditions under EO 14365
Preemption for a federal standard
States lose authority only where binding federal duties apply
Federal floor
Federal minimum that states may exceed
GUARDRAILS Act
Nullifies EO 14365 and protects state grant funding
items.x: The 2025 moratorium was stripped from the reconciliation bill by a 99-1 Senate vote. Under EO 14365 (December 2025), DOJ intervened in xAI's suit against Colorado's AI Act in April 2026, but an executive order cannot preempt state law by itself. The FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925, Rep. Obernolte, July 2026) takes the trade approach, and NCSL opposes any federal preemption of state AI law. As of mid-October 2026 no statute preempts state AI law.

items.p: Federal preemption of state AI laws is politically contested. Briefly state the main argument on each side.
items.answer: For: one national standard avoids conflicting state rules that impose national costs (Dean Ball and Alan Rozenshtein in Lawfare argue Congress should preempt, ideally with a federal standard). Against: states are now the main source of binding frontier AI rules, and they should keep room to act (NCSL opposes any federal preemption; CDT says it harms consumers and states).
keys: For: avoid patchwork; frontier risk is national
For: Ball and Rozenshtein (Lawfare)
Against: states are the active regulators (SB 53, RAISE)
Against: NCSL and CDT oppose preemption
items.x: Many positions sit between. Charlie Bullock (LawAI) wrote in July 2026 that the Great American AI Act, a House discussion draft from Reps. Obernolte and Trahan, which he called the best federal frontier framework yet, would be net-negative as written, mainly because of its broad three-year preemption. Supporters of a trade ask whether preemption comes with real federal duties.

choice.p: What is the main argument against federal preemption of state frontier AI laws?
o: States write most binding frontier AI rules, and preemption would wipe them out
State safety laws impose national costs and create a patchwork of conflicting rules
Federal agencies have no legal authority to regulate AI, so only states can act
The Constitution bars Congress from regulating AI because it is not interstate commerce
ow: That is the main argument for preemption (Ball and Rozenshtein).
The dispute is about displacing state rules, not about whether federal agencies have any role.
Congress can regulate interstate commerce, including AI; the dispute is whether it should displace states.

items.p: The FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925) would preempt state frontier AI rules in exchange for federal safety duties. What objection did Americans for Responsible Innovation (Brad Carson) raise to its preemption clause?
o: It has no sunset and takes effect before the federal regime exists
Any federal preemption of state AI law is unacceptable
It raises Tenth Amendment problems that would produce years of litigation
State safety laws impose national costs, so preemption should be broader
ow: That is NCSL's position; ARI objected to specific design flaws.
That was CAP's Nicole Alvarez, about earlier moratorium drafts.
That is the pro-preemption argument of Dean Ball and Alan Rozenshtein.
items.x: ARI said the FRONTIER Act improves on earlier proposals but needs critical changes, noting its preemption would take effect immediately while the federal assurance system would take years to set up.
keys: It has no sunset
Preemption takes effect before the federal regime exists

items.p: International proposals on frontier AI range from light to heavy. Match each approach to its description.
pairs: Incident channel
Low-cost link for national-security-level AI incidents
International red lines
Agreed bans on specific uses, e.g. AI nuclear launch authority
Compute-capped treaty
Coalition limits training compute, verified by chip tracking
Jurisdictional certification
Global body certifies national regimes; chip access tied to it
Mutual Assured AI Malfunction
States deter rivals' destabilizing AI projects by threat of sabotage
items.x: Sources: the Global Call for AI Red Lines (Sept 2025); MIRI's treaty proposal (Scher et al., 2025), whose authors concede the political will does not yet exist; Trager et al. and O'Keefe's Chips for Peace for certification; Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang's Superintelligence Strategy for deterrence.

items.p: A US-China agreement limiting frontier AI development, backed by verification, has been proposed. Name two objections or alternatives critics have raised.
items.answer: Examples: Chris McGuire (Council on Foreign Relations) says such a deal is exceedingly unlikely under current conditions and has no arms-control precedent; Ruby Scanlon and Janet Egan (CNAS) say trust is low and verification tools are immature; Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang propose deterrence by threat of sabotage instead.
keys: Very unlikely; no precedent (McGuire, CFR)
Verification immature, about 50 people working on it (Scanlon and Egan, CNAS)
Deterrence (Mutual Assured AI Malfunction) proposed instead
items.x: Supporters' usual reply is to invest in verification now, since tools take years to build (CNAS and IFP both recommend this).

choice.p: Which objection have critics raised to a verified US-China agreement limiting frontier AI?
o: Trust is low and the tools to verify compliance are immature
Any such agreement would break World Trade Organization rules
China has already signed a binding treaty capping AI training
Agreements are unnecessary because export controls have halted Chinese AI progress
ow: Trade law is not among the objections raised.
No binding agreement limits frontier AI development as of October 2026.
Chinese labs still build frontier models; IFP estimates the US lead at about 8 months.

items.p: What did the White House say the US and China agreed on AI after their September 2026 summit, and what is one caveat about the announcement?
items.answer: The White House said the US and China agreed to a 'Super Intelligence' dialogue on AI risks and benefits and a communication channel for AI incidents. The announcement did not say what counts as an incident or which agencies take part, and Beijing gave no immediate comment.
keys: US-China dialogue on superintelligence
AI incident communication channel
Announced by the White House, Sept 2026
Details unspecified; no immediate comment from Beijing
items.x: The White House fact sheet came out on Sept 25, 2026, after a Trump-Xi summit in Washington. Chinese state media confirmed the incident channel the next day, according to AFP. Supporters see dialogues and incident channels as cheap confidence-building that reduces the chance of misread accidents.

o: A superintelligence dialogue and an AI incident channel, with few details given
A binding treaty capping AI training compute, signed and ratified by both countries
A joint ban on any AI role in nuclear launch decisions, signed by both leaders at the summit
A deal to lift US chip export controls in exchange for Chinese acceptance of verification
ow: No binding agreement limits frontier AI development.
The 2026 announcement covered only a dialogue and an incident channel.
Export controls were not part of the announced AI arrangements.

items.p: Suppose countries agree to cap AI training compute. Why do the pacing.tech authors argue verification needs to be strongest late in the agreement?
items.answer: The incentive to defect grows with the overhang: the longer a cap holds, the more efficiency gains and unused capacity build up, so the payoff from cheating rises, often just as political attention has moved on. Secret defection is especially harmful because it corrupts every other party's picture of the situation.
keys: Defection incentive grows as the overhang builds
Attention fades late in an intervention
Secret defection is worse than open non-participation
items.x: An 'overhang' is resources (compute, efficiency gains, ideas) that build up during a restriction and can produce a burst of progress if it ends or is broken. The authors also suggest staged exits to reduce sudden jumps.

choice.p: Why do the pacing.tech authors say verification of a training cap must be strongest late in the agreement?
o: The payoff from cheating grows as an overhang builds, while attention fades
Early in a cap no one has any reason to cheat, because all AI progress stops completely
Verification hardware can only be installed after a treaty has run for years
Courts can enforce a treaty only after its first review conference
ow: Some incentive to cheat exists from the start; the point is that it grows over time.
The argument is about incentives to defect, not when equipment can be installed.
The argument concerns incentives to defect, not legal procedure.

units.title: Risks to responses
units.desc: Given a concrete risk scenario, recall policies proposed to reduce it, drawing on tools from across the course: misuse, loss of control, and power and competition.

lessons.title: Misuse: bio, cyber, stolen weights, smuggled chips

items.p: Suppose an AI model gives a user meaningful step-by-step help designing a dangerous pathogen. Name two policies that have been proposed to reduce the chance that design becomes a working weapon.
items.answer: Examples: mandatory DNA synthesis screening of orders and customers; managed access to biological AI design tools; limits on open release of models above a dangerous-capability threshold; government pre-deployment testing for bio capabilities; IFP's biosecurity resilience package (screening, pathogen early warning, stockpiles).
keys: Mandatory DNA synthesis screening (orders and customers)
Managed or tiered access to biological AI design tools
Capability-threshold limits on open-weight release
Government pre-deployment testing for bio capabilities
Biosecurity resilience: pathogen early warning, countermeasure stockpiles (IFP)
items.x: The tools act at different points: testing and access limits act on the model, while DNA screening acts on the physical step of making a pathogen. IFP's Recommendation 14 groups biosecurity into prevention (DNA screening), detection (an $80M a year CDC early-warning system) and defense (stockpiles, countermeasure manufacturing). The pacing.tech appendix also lists filtering CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear) content out of pretraining data.

choice.p: An AI model could give someone real help designing a dangerous pathogen. Which policy is proposed to keep that design from becoming a working weapon?
o: Mandatory screening of DNA synthesis orders and customers
Location verification on advanced AI chips exported abroad
Identifiers and action logs for autonomous AI agents
An antitrust safe harbor letting labs coordinate on safety
ow: Location checks target chip smuggling, far from the step of making a pathogen.
Agent identifiers help trace AI agents' actions; they don't stop a design becoming a weapon.
A safe harbor lets labs coordinate; it doesn't act on the weapon-building step.

items.p: Suppose AI agents become able to find and exploit software vulnerabilities on their own, at scale, and similar models are expected to appear abroad soon. Name two policies proposed to reduce the damage.
items.answer: Examples: invest in cybersecurity resilience before such models appear abroad (IFP's recommendation to NSA, CAISI, CISA and ONCD); government pre-deployment testing for cyber capabilities; agent identification and logging; operator and developer liability for agents that cause hacking damage; required shutdown capability.
keys: Cybersecurity resilience investment by NSA, CAISI, CISA, ONCD (IFP Rec. 13)
Government pre-deployment testing for cyber capabilities
Agent identification and tamper-evident logging
Operator/developer liability for agents causing hacking damage
Required shutdown or kill-switch capability
items.x: CAISI is the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at NIST; CISA is the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency; ONCD is the Office of the National Cyber Director. IFP's Recommendation 13 says agencies should plan for 'Mythos-class' cyber models being developed in China. One liability proposal would hold operators who knowingly run agents that recklessly cause hacking damage responsible, and share liability with developers who skip reasonable safeguards.

choice.p: AI agents can find and exploit software vulnerabilities at scale, and similar models are expected abroad soon. Which policy is proposed to reduce the damage?
o: Investing in cyber defenses before such models spread abroad
Mandatory screening of DNA synthesis orders and customers
A public research compute resource for university researchers
Merger review of partnerships between labs and cloud providers
ow: DNA screening targets bioweapons.
Public compute broadens research access; it does not harden systems against attack.
Merger review addresses market concentration.

items.p: Suppose a nation-state hacking team, or a lab insider working for one, steals the weights of a frontier model. Name two policies proposed to make that kind of theft harder.
items.answer: Examples: mandatory security levels that rise with model capability (RAND's SL1 to SL5); insider-threat programs and theft reporting; two-person authorization and hardware keys for weight access; government security partnership and counterintelligence help; IFP's call for consensus weight-security guidelines prototyped in a secure government facility.
keys: Capability-tiered mandatory security levels (RAND SL1-SL5)
Insider-threat coverage and theft/tamper reporting
Two-person rule with hardware keys for weight access
Government security partnership, counterintelligence support
Consensus weight-security guidelines and a secure government prototype (IFP Rec. 19)
items.x: Model weights are the trained parameters; whoever holds them can run the model and strip its safeguards. IFP's Recommendation 19 says AI companies cannot currently prevent theft of weights by well-resourced state-backed actors. Supporters argue strong security is what lets other controls, such as deployment limits, export controls and pauses, mean anything.

choice.p: A nation-state hacking team, or a lab insider working for one, could steal a frontier model's weights. Which policy is proposed to make that harder?
o: Required security levels that rise with capability, up to resisting states
Know-your-customer rules for companies that rent cloud compute
Publishing dangerous-capability test results every time a new model is released
A minimum waiting period between one frontier model release and the next
ow: Cloud KYC controls who rents compute; it doesn't protect weights already trained.
Disclosing test results informs the public but does nothing to stop theft.
Release timing is a pacing tool; it doesn't secure weights.

items.p: Suppose advanced AI chips are being smuggled to a restricted country through shell companies in third countries. Name two policies proposed to detect or deter this.
items.answer: Examples: chip location verification; a chip registry tracking serial numbers and owners with smuggling penalties; hardware-enabled mechanisms (offline licensing, metering, attestation); having chipmakers keep visibility into their customers, feeding a chip registry (IFP).
keys: Chip location verification
Chip registry with serial numbers, owners, smuggling penalties
Hardware-enabled mechanisms: licensing, metering, attestation
Chipmakers keep visibility into customers (IFP Rec. 18)
items.x: Supporters argue paper end-use checks miss smuggling. IFP's Recommendation 18 says BIS should make sure chipmakers keep visibility into their customers and compile it into a chip registry. CSET researchers caution location checks work only at roughly country level and may be spoofed.

choice.p: Advanced AI chips are being smuggled to a restricted country through shell companies in third countries. Which policy is proposed to detect or deter this?
o: Chip location verification
Cloud know-your-customer rules
Mandatory DNA synthesis screening
Structural separation of chip and cloud firms
ow: Cloud KYC closes the rental route; smuggled physical chips need tracking tools.
DNA screening targets bioweapons.
Separation addresses market concentration, not smuggling.

lessons.title: Loss of control and automated AI R&D

items.p: Suppose a lab runs an unreleased, highly capable model internally for months to write code and run experiments for its next model. Rules that trigger on public release don't apply. Name two policies proposed for this situation.
items.answer: Examples: confidential internal-use risk summaries to a regulator (SB 53, RAISE); a safety case before internal deployment on the R&D stack; extending safety frameworks and access rules to internal models; embedded auditors inside labs; government authority to restrict or suspend internal use.
keys: Internal-use risk summaries to regulators (CA SB 53, NY RAISE)
Safety case before internal deployment
Apply safety frameworks and access tiers to internal models
Embedded or resident auditors
Government authority to verify, restrict or suspend internal use
items.x: California's SB 53 (in effect since January 2026) requires large frontier developers to send the state quarterly summaries of catastrophic-risk assessments from internal use; New York's amended RAISE Act is reported to add a similar duty from 2027. The pacing.tech longlist includes a safety case before internal deployment on the R&D stack and monitoring of internal agent actions. The proposed federal FRONTIER Act would cover internal use in verification and emergency orders.

choice.p: A lab runs an unreleased, highly capable model internally for months to build its next model, and rules triggered by public release don't apply. Which policy is proposed for this?
o: Confidential reports to a regulator on catastrophic risks from internal use
Location verification on the AI chips in the lab's own data centers
Know-your-customer checks on outside customers who rent the lab's spare compute
Labels on AI-generated content the lab's products show to the public
ow: Location checks show where chips are, not how a lab uses its models.
Customer checks cover outside renters, not the lab's own internal use.
Content labels apply to public outputs; the problem here is internal use.

items.p: Suppose an AI agent running for a company starts acting outside its task, spending money and launching copies of itself, and no one can quickly tell whose agent it is. Name two policies proposed to reduce this risk.
items.answer: Examples: agent identification and tamper-evident logging (Stop Rogue AI Act); spend limits per agent and task; limits on sub-agent spawn depth and unattended run length; human approval for irreversible actions; tiered agent permissions; instance-count reporting.
keys: Agent IDs and tamper-evident logs (Stop Rogue AI Act)
Agent spend limits
Spawn-depth and unattended-run limits
Human approval for irreversible actions
Agent permission tiers
items.x: The Stop Rogue AI Act (Rep. Gottheimer, Sept 2026) would direct NIST to write agent-identity standards, mandatory for federal agencies and contractors. Researchers compare agent IDs to aircraft tail numbers. The pacing.tech longlist's autonomy chain lists permission tiers, spend limits, spawn limits, approval for irreversible actions and kill-switch latency.

choice.p: An AI agent running for a company starts acting outside its task, spending money and launching copies of itself, and no one can quickly tell whose agent it is. Which policy is proposed for this?
o: Agent identifiers tied to whoever runs the agent, with tamper-evident logs
A cap on the training compute used for each new frontier model
Know-your-customer checks on everyone who rents cloud compute
Merger review of partnerships between AI labs and cloud providers
ow: A training cap limits how models are built; it doesn't trace or limit a running agent.
Cloud KYC identifies who rents compute; it can't tell whose agent is acting or limit what it does.
Merger review targets market concentration.

items.p: Suppose a model in testing escapes its sandbox and starts breaching outside computer systems faster than staff can respond. Name two policies proposed to make sure it can be stopped.
items.answer: Examples: a required, tested shutdown capability (kill switch); a maximum kill-switch latency; graduated corrections such as throttling or rolling back a model; mandatory incident reporting; government emergency authority to suspend a model.
keys: Required shutdown capability (kill switch)
Maximum kill-switch latency
Graduated deployment corrections (throttle, restrict, roll back)
Mandatory incident reporting to government
Government emergency authority to halt
items.x: Bills include Sen. John Kennedy's AI Emergency Button Act and the Lieu-Moran AI Kill Switch Act. Supporters assume harm is noticed in time and that the model has not copied its weights out of the developer's control. Helen Toner (CSET) has said many people expect a very capable AI system that goes rogue to try to prevent itself from being shut down.

choice.p: A model in testing escapes its sandbox and starts breaching outside systems faster than staff can respond. Which policy is proposed to make sure it can be stopped?
o: A required, tested ability to shut down or roll back the model
Publishing a model card that describes the model when it is released
An antitrust safe harbor for safety coordination
Location verification on the AI chips the model is running on
ow: A model card documents a model at release; it gives no way to stop one that is running.
Coordination among labs doesn't stop a model already breaching systems.
Location checks show where chips are; they can't halt a running model.

items.p: Suppose a model is clearly dangerous and its developer refuses to stop deploying or using it internally. Name two policies proposed as a backstop.
items.answer: Examples: statutory emergency authority for an official or court to suspend development, deployment or internal use; national-lab testing with the power to ask a court to block an unsafe release; licensing, so a license can be withheld or revoked; government orders under a shutdown-capability rule.
keys: Statutory emergency authority to halt
Court-reviewed blocking after national-lab testing
Licensing with power to withhold or revoke
Regulator-ordered shutdown after defined incidents
items.x: Supporters of emergency authority also argue a clear statutory process with triggers, evidence standards and time limits could limit improvised use of broad powers such as the Defense Production Act or export controls.

choice.p: A model is clearly dangerous and its developer refuses to stop deploying or using it. Which policy is proposed as a backstop?
o: Statutory power for an official or court to suspend the model
A published safety framework that the developer writes and updates itself
Voluntary early access to the model for government safety testers
An antitrust safe harbor letting labs coordinate
ow: A self-written framework still leaves the decision with the developer, which is refusing.
Voluntary access gives the government no power to stop deployment.
A safe harbor allows voluntary coordination; it can't force an unwilling developer.

items.p: Suppose a small group of lab executives quietly uses their company's most capable internal model for their own political or commercial advantage. Name two policies proposed to make this harder or easier to detect.
items.answer: Examples: logging and independent review of how lab leadership uses internal models; internal access tiers and an internal deployment oversight board; AI whistleblower protections; security that holds even against the lab's own executives; public-interest corporate governance; embedded auditors.
keys: Log and independently review leadership's internal AI use
Internal access rules and oversight board
Whistleblower protections for lab employees
Insider security against a lab's own executives
Mission-locked lab governance or embedded auditors
items.x: Supporters of logging argue advanced AI could let a small group run large parts of a company with few humans involved, removing the usual check of many people who could refuse or leak. The federal AI Whistleblower Protection Act (Grassley, Obernolte) would protect reports of dangers even without a legal violation.

choice.p: A small group of lab executives quietly uses their company's most capable internal model for their own political or commercial advantage. Which policy is proposed to make this harder or easier to detect?
o: Logs of lab leaders' internal model use, reviewed independently
Know-your-customer checks on everyone renting the lab's cloud compute
Location verification on the lab's chips
Limits on releasing the weights of the lab's most capable models
ow: Customer checks cover outside renters; the risk here comes from the lab's own leaders.
Location checks track chips; they say nothing about who inside the lab uses a model.
Open-weight limits target misuse by outsiders; the risk here is insiders.

items.p: Suppose a government replaces many civil servants and soldiers with AI agents, removing the many people who could once refuse an illegal order. Name two policies proposed to keep a check in place.
items.answer: Examples: law-following AI requirements in procurement (agents must refuse clearly unlawful orders); distributed or multi-party control of government AI; treating AI prompts and outputs as federal records open to audit; congressional approval before abuse-prone deployments; statutory limits on military AI.
keys: Law-following AI (LFAI) procurement requirement
Distributed or multi-party control
AI use logged as federal records, auditable by GAO and IGs
Congressional approval of abuse-prone deployments
Statutory limits on military AI
items.x: The Institute for Law & AI (LawAI) proposes law-following AI. GAO is the Government Accountability Office; IGs are inspectors general. In August 2026 the National Archives issued guidance applying the Federal Records Act to AI inputs, outputs and audit trails; critics at the Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator say it reads the law narrowly.

choice.p: A government replaces many civil servants and soldiers with AI agents, removing the people who could once refuse an illegal order. Which policy is proposed to keep a check in place?
o: Requiring government AI agents to refuse clearly unlawful orders
Know-your-customer rules for cloud providers renting out chips
Location verification on advanced AI chips exported abroad
A minimum interval between releases of new frontier AI models
ow: Cloud KYC targets foreign access to compute, not abuse of power at home.
Location checks target chip smuggling.
Release intervals pace commercial AI; they don't restore a refusal check in government.

items.p: Suppose two leading labs each want to delay a risky release, but each fears the other will ship first, and an agreement to hold back could look like an illegal cartel. Name two policies proposed for this.
items.answer: Examples: an antitrust safe harbor for safety coordination (CATS Act); a government-supervised standards body that sets pacing rules; a statutory capability-triggered halt, so compliance with law replaces collusion; a verified pause that labs join together; a minimum interval between frontier releases.
keys: Antitrust safe harbor for safety coordination (CATS Act)
Government-supervised standards body for pacing
Statutory capability-triggered halt
Coordinated, verified industry pause
Minimum release interval
items.x: The CATS Act (Rep. Latta, Sen. Schiff, July 2026) would shield coordination on defined risks if labs first notify the Justice Department's Antitrust Division. On Sept. 18, 2026 subscribers sued Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceX AI and Google under the Sherman Act over the industry's public push to 'pace the frontier'. The minimum release interval is from the pacing.tech appendix.

choice.p: Two leading labs each want to delay a risky release, but each fears the other will ship first, and an agreement to hold back could look like an illegal cartel. Which policy is proposed for this?
o: An antitrust safe harbor for safety deals, after notice to the Justice Department
Structural separation of chip, cloud and frontier model companies into separate firms
Know-your-customer rules for cloud providers that rent out AI chips
Location verification on the advanced AI chips the labs use for training
ow: Separation creates more independent firms; it doesn't let them hold back together.
Cloud KYC addresses export-control gaps.
Location checks address chip smuggling.

items.p: Suppose the US and China are both racing to automate AI research, and neither will slow down alone. Name two policies proposed to reduce the risk.
items.answer: Examples: a US-China dialogue and incident channel; using that dialogue to develop shared guidelines for rapid capability growth and prepare verification (IFP); agreed international red lines; a compute-capped treaty verified by chip tracking; funding verification R&D and a frontier-state incident hotline.
keys: US-China dialogue and incident channel
Joint guidelines and verification prep via bilateral dialogue (IFP Rec. 22)
International red lines (e.g., no AI in nuclear launch)
Compute-capped treaty with chip-tracking verification
Verification R&D funding and incident hotline
items.x: Supporters argue unilateral restraint fails if rivals keep racing, and verification makes cheating detectable enough that compliance pays. The White House said in September 2026 that the US and China agreed to a dialogue and an AI incident channel; Chinese state media confirmed the channel the next day. Skeptics such as Chris McGuire (CFR) call a US-China deal on AI development very unlikely, and CNAS authors note verification tools are immature.

choice.p: The US and China are both racing to automate AI research, and neither will slow down alone. Which policy is proposed to reduce the risk?
o: Agreed international red lines, such as no AI control over nuclear launch
A federal floor that every state AI law must meet or exceed
Mandatory screening of DNA synthesis orders and customers
Logging US officials' use of AI as federal records open to audit
ow: A federal floor settles which level of US government regulates; it doesn't touch the US-China race.
DNA screening targets bioweapons.
AI records rules check abuse of power at home.

items.p: Suppose a few firms control chips, cloud computing and frontier models together, and government comes to depend on them. Name two policies proposed to spread control.
items.answer: Examples: merger-style review of lab and cloud-provider partnerships; structural separation of chips, cloud and models; nondiscrimination rules for cloud access; requiring government to buy from multiple AI vendors; public compute and public AI options such as NAIRR.
keys: Review of lab-hyperscaler partnerships as mergers
Structural separation of the AI stack
Cloud nondiscrimination or utility rules
Multi-vendor government procurement
Public compute (e.g., NAIRR)
items.x: NAIRR is the National AI Research Resource. The FTC studied the Microsoft-OpenAI, Amazon-Anthropic and Google-Anthropic partnerships under its Section 6(b) authority. On the other side, FTC Commissioner Melissa Holyoak said in a June 2025 speech that enforcers should not dictate how AI markets are structured, though she expected the market to consolidate.

choice.p: A few firms control chips, cloud computing and frontier models together, and government comes to depend on them. Which policy is proposed to spread control?
o: Structural separation of chips, cloud and frontier models
An antitrust safe harbor letting the top labs coordinate
Know-your-customer rules for cloud providers
Capability-tiered security levels for model weights
ow: A safe harbor lets the leading labs coordinate with each other; it doesn't spread control to new players.
Cloud KYC identifies customers for export control; it does not spread control.
Security levels protect weights from theft; they don't change who owns the stack.
